## Beloved Reader!

That this little work <note>German: *Werkchen*; a humble diminutive often used by 18th and 19th-century authors to describe their publications</note> might please you, and that it might achieve its purpose to be both useful and pleasant, is the sole wish of the authors; the fulfillment of this wish will reward them for their efforts. — You will find little here that is original, but all the more pearls gathered which, until now, have not been found by everyone. Most were fished from the Orient <note>Refers generally to the Middle East and surrounding regions in this historical context</note>, and this distant fishing is not everyone’s business — That the fishermen, who herewith deliver their catch to you, are well acquainted with the Orient and its languages, you may modestly discern from several pieces of their collection, which

## Dialogues.
### I.

### on
### World, Being, Creation, Production, and Preservation of Beings.

->From a Shastra <term>Shastra: From the Sanskrit "śāstra," referring to a treatise, manual, or body of sacred Hindu teachings.</term> or old commentary of a Brahmin <note>A member of the highest Hindu caste, traditionally serving as priests and scholars.</note> on the Indian law-books, the Vedas <note>original: "Wedam"</note>.<-

---

### Biasche. <note>Likely representing Vyasa, the legendary sage credited with compiling the Vedas.</note>

**W**hereon in particular should one direct one's attention when considering the various beings <note>original: "Wesen"; can refer to entities, essences, or living things</note> of which this world is composed?

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page where Biasche asked Schumontu how one should study the world. Here, Schumontu provides a systematic framework for understanding the nature of existence, echoing the categorical logic found in classical Indian philosophy, particularly the Vaisheshika school.</meta>

## Schumontu.

If one wishes to know the essence <note>original: "Wesen"; here meaning the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> of every thing precisely, then seven points <note>original: "Stücke," meaning parts or aspects of an argument</note> primarily come into consideration. This knowledge leads us imperceptibly and surely to that of the true God. Above all things, one must consider the being in itself, seek to research its nature, and then its characteristics and properties: whether it be capable of action <note>original: "Handlung"</note> or not, whether it be composite or simple; in what it agrees with other beings; or what unique qualities it possesses. One counts in general nine categories <note>original: "Gattungen"</note> of beings: the earth, the water, the light, the wind, the air, the time, the regions of the world <note>Refers to the cardinal directions or space</note>, the soul, and the will. Then the characteristics of each being are considered: whether it is sentient or not; whether it constitutes only one or several in number; whether it is composed of several inseparable or separable parts; what it has in common with others, or what is peculiar to it; how large it is, and finally whether it is capable of intellect <note>original: "Verstand"</note>, joy, pain, desire, hate, reflection, and memory. All of these are so many characteristics. To move something upward or downward,

<vocab>Being, pieces/points, consideration, knowledge, nature, characteristics, properties, action, categories, earth, water, light, wind, air, time, world-regions, soul, will, intellect, joy, pain, desire, hate, reflection, memory</vocab>

<summary>Schumontu explains that understanding the essence of all things leads to the knowledge of God, outlining nine categories of existence and the various qualities used to analyze them. This framework attempts to map the physical and mental world through a specific philosophical lens.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, categories of existence, natural philosophy, theology, Vaisheshika, elements, soul, intellect</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Biasche and Schumontu, expanding on the definitions of the nine categories of beings introduced on the previous page. The text continues the previous page’s final sentence regarding types of action.</meta>

...away, to open, to conclude, to go, to come, and so forth. This is what one calls an **action**.

### Biasche.

Now I know what must be investigated in every matter; but I would also like to learn from you, what then is actually the particular **essence** <note>original: "Wesen"; the fundamental nature of a substance</note> of each thing?

### Schumontu.

In her womb, the earth contains the seed, the germ of every tree, of every fragrant flower. Therefore, its essence has been designated with the term <term>Gondopoti</term> <note>Likely a corruption of the Sanskrit "Gandhavati," meaning "possessing fragrance," a classic attribute of the element Earth in Indian philosophy</note>, which means a queen of fragrances. Fluidity and coolness constitute the essence of water; touch <note>The sensation of feeling/impact</note> that of the wind. The essence of the air consists in the fact that it transmits sound and propagates it to us; that of light, that it enables us to notice and distinguish color. The susceptibility to pleasure and pain constitutes the essence of the soul. Memory that of the will. Moreover, all these properties of which I speak here do not belong to the essence of things, but are merely, as it were, **supports** <note>original: "Stüzzen"; possibly referring to accidental qualities that depend on the substance</note> of the same.

| :--- | :--- |
| Biasche | Pupil or interlocutor |

| Gondopoti | "Queen of Fragrances" (Earth) |
| Erde | Earth |
| Wasser | Water |
| Wind | Wind/Touch |
| Luft | Air/Sound |
| Licht | Light/Color |
| Seele | Soul |
| Stüzzen | Supports/Accidental properties |

<summary>Schumontu defines the specific essences of the natural elements and the soul, attributing unique sensory qualities like fragrance to earth, sound to air, and color to light. He clarifies that while these traits define the things, they are merely 'supports' of the deeper essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the sage Schumontu and his pupil Biasche. Having previously defined the categories of existence and the nature of the elements, they now move toward the ultimate purpose of this knowledge: understanding the nature of the Divine through the process of elimination.</meta>

## Biasche.

But why all of this? What is the use of it?

## Schumontu.

Without knowing all this, it is impossible to arrive at a knowledge of the essence of God. All these branches of knowledge are therefore absolutely necessary. Once one possesses them, the conclusion is easy: that which is none of these things is God. <note>This refers to the "Via Negativa" or *Neti Neti* ("not this, not that") approach in theology, where God is defined by what He is not—He is beyond physical elements, senses, and categories.</note>

## Biasche.

I feel the truth of what you tell me; yet I still require more detailed instruction. Teach me more precisely: what is that which is called a **creature** <note>original: "Geschöpf"; referring to any created being or thing</note>, and who is the **Creator**? What is the intention behind all of this, and where does it all lead? Furthermore, explain to me: what is the soul, and what is a **work of magic** <note>original: "Zauberwerk"; in this context, it likely refers to *Maya*, the cosmic illusion that makes the temporary world appear real</note>? Who was Pokriti <note>Sanskrit: *Prakriti*, meaning Nature or the primal female creative energy</note>, the first woman *), and who was her husband? With what qualities did God equip them at the very beginning? And where was their dwelling? Who—

...to teach them a better way. ### Biasche.

Whom do you call virtuous? I, at least, know of none? —

### Schumontu.

Indeed, there are! There are still many virtuous people on the earth. Whoever loves the truth, whoever reads only the Veda and instructs people in it, whoever prays only the prayers prescribed in the Veda; whoever seeks enlightenment in this book alone, and whoever is compassionate toward sinners and the poor—it is your duty to strive for the company and friendship of such a person.

### Biasche.

This is how the scholars arrange the location of the various regions of the Earth. The sea surrounds them all, except for the place inhabited by the Supreme Being.

...darkness and night. In the month of December, it <note>The sun (German: *die Sonne*) is grammatically feminine in the original text.</note> moves into the south, where it remains for six months. ### Sumantu. <note>Original: "Schumontu."</note>

### Sumantu.

Everything is, as it were, visibly in growth, and the air, cooled by the frequent rain, revitalizes humans and animals anew.

# Vyasa. <note>Original: "Biasche."</note>

Once Brahma, the father of Manu, <note>Original: "Munu."</note> prayed to Vishnu, the Supreme Being. The latter listened to him favorably and asked what he desired. "How," replied Brahma, "do you wish me to bring forth creatures? The entire earth is flooded; there is no place where they can remain." Upon this, Vishnu made the decision to embody himself, specifically in the body of a boar. <note>Original: "Sau," literally sow, but referring here to the Varaha or Boar avatar.</note> At his birth, he was scarcely an inch tall, but he soon reached the size of an elephant. Pulastya, Marichi, Atri, Angiras, <note>Original: "Pulastudu, Morise, Otri, Onguiro." The God who is the creator and sustainer of this universe is eternal by his very nature, and yet you would have him be born? <meta>This page provides the answer to the question posed by Vyasa at the end of the previous page. Having heard the terrors of hell, Vyasa asked how to escape them; the sage Sumantu now explains that only sincere repentance and a change of heart can offer a path to salvation.</meta>

### Sumantu <note>Original: "Schumontu." A legendary sage and student of Vyasa, often depicted as a teacher of sacred wisdom.</note>

Through nothing other than immediate repentance. <note>The German "Busse" implies both the internal feeling of remorse and the external act of penance or atonement.</note> Whoever delays it until death will be forced to perform it in hell for all eternity.

But if repentance is to be truly fruitful, it must be joined with a complete and sincere resolution not to fall back into previous errors; otherwise, it is of no use at all.

To strive for the forgiveness of sins through repentance while still maintaining the will to commit them again is to be like an elephant that, after being washed in a river, rolls in the mud <note>Original: "Pfütze" (puddle). This is a traditional Indian metaphor (Gaja-snāna) for a purification that is rendered useless by the immediate return to worldly or sinful habits.</note> as soon as it has left the water.

What could it possibly help to make empty promises to God, who searches the heart and sees through its most secret folds, or to merely adopt the outward appearance of virtue in His presence?

Begin by making a firm and sincere resolution to sin no more, if you wish for me to fully complete my instruction on the qualities of true repentance.

Only God can forgive our sins: to imploringly pray for His mercy, to [win] it through good works—

<meta>catchword: win [winnen],</meta>

<summary>Sumantu explains that the only way to escape the punishments of hell is through immediate and sincere repentance, which requires a genuine commitment to avoid future sin. He warns that performative virtue is useless before God, who sees the true state of the heart.</summary>
<keywords>repentance, forgiveness, sincerity, divine judgment, Sumantu, sin, virtue, elephant metaphor</keywords>

—win it, to earn it through pure love for Him; that, then, is what you must strive for.

## Vyasa <note>Original: "Biasche." Vyasa is a central and revered figure in Hindu tradition, credited as the compiler of the Vedas and the author of the Mahabharata.</note>

What is meant by a "good work"? And the love of God—in what does it consist?

## Sumantu <note>Original: "Schumontu." In this context, he acts as the teacher providing the "accessible" version of the sacred laws.</note>

To do what the <term>Veda</term> <note>Original: "Wedam." The Vedas are the oldest and most authoritative scriptures of Hinduism, encompassing hymns, philosophy, and guidance for rituals.</note> prescribes, and to do it exactly as it prescribes—this is what is called a "good work." As for the love of God: there are four types. To love God above all things, for His own sake, without desire and unselfishly—that is the first and most excellent kind of love for God. To strive to conquer oneself, and to find one's greatest pleasure in meditating on the perfection of God and in His glorification—this is what the second kind of love for God consists of; it is somewhat more imperfect than the first because it is not entirely free from personal desire and self-interest. It is also still considered loving God, albeit imperfectly, when one is subject to the passions and feels their yoke and dominion, yet in such a way that one always returns to God from time to time and glorifies His greatness. That is the—

<note>Original vocabulary list: Vyasa, Sumantu, Veda, Love of God, Perfection, Passions.</note>

<summary>Sumantu defines a good work as adherence to Vedic prescriptions and begins to categorize the love of God into four distinct levels based on their purity and lack of self-interest. He describes the highest love as completely selfless, while lower forms involve a struggle against the passions or a lingering sense of personal desire.</summary>
<keywords>Vyasa, Sumantu, Veda, good works, love of God, devotion, spiritual hierarchy, perfection, passions</keywords>

# Brahma and Narada,
## a
## Conversation between Eternal Wisdom and Reason.

->From the Vedanga Shastra <term>Bedang Schaster: Likely referring to the Vedangas, the six auxiliary disciplines of Hinduism that developed in ancient times and are connected with the study of the Vedas.</term>, a commentary on the Vedas <term>Wedam: An archaic spelling of the Vedas, the oldest and most sacred scriptures of Hinduism.</term>.<-

### Narada <note>Narada is a divine sage in Hindu tradition, often described as the son of Brahma. Here, the translator frames him as the personification of Reason.</note>.

O Father! You, the first from God, are said to have created the world; and your son Narada, full of wonder at what he sees, desires to be instructed on how all these things were made.

### Brahma <note>Brahma, the creator god in the Hindu Trimurti. Here, he is framed as the personification of Eternal Wisdom.</note>.

Do not be mistaken, my son! and do not imagine that I am the creator of the world and independent of the divine Mover, who is the great primordial Being and the creator of all things. Therefore, look upon me only as the instrument of the great Will and as a part of his essence, which he called forth to fulfill his eternal purposes.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical dialogue between Brahma (Eternal Wisdom) and Narada (Reason). ### Narada.

->What then should we think of God?<-

### Brahma.

Since he is without matter <term>matter: In this context, "Materie" refers to physical substance or "Prakriti," contrasting with the purely spiritual nature of the supreme deity.</term>, he is beyond all imagination. Since he is invisible, he can have no form.

But from what we see in his works, we can conclude that he is eternal, almighty, omniscient, and omnipresent.

### Narada.

->How did God create the world?<-

### Brahma.

Love dwelt with God from eternity. It was of three different kinds: the creative, the sustaining, and the destroying <note>original: "verderbende." While "verderben" often means to spoil or decay, in the context of the Hindu Trimurti, it refers to the necessary cycle of destruction and transformation led by Shiva.</note>. ## Brimha.

His eyes can be compared with the lotus to show that they are always open, like this flower, which cannot be submerged by the greatest depth of water. <note>The lotus is a central symbol in Indian philosophy; because it floats on the water's surface while its roots are in the mud, it represents divine purity and detachment from the material world.</note> His skin, like a cloud, is a symbol of the darkness with which he veils himself from mortal eyes. <note>This refers to the "dark" or "sky-blue" complexion (Sanskrit: *shyam*) traditionally attributed to Vishnu and Krishna, representing the infinite and the unmanifested.</note> His garment is like lightning, in order to express the venerable majesty that surrounds him. <note>A reference to the *Pitambara*, the radiant yellow silken robe of Vishnu, which is often compared to the brilliance of the sun or lightning.</note> His four hands depict his strength and almighty power.

### Brahma.

God does not eat or drink like a mortal man. However, if you do not love God, your offerings will not be worthy of him. For since all men desire the good things of this world for themselves, God requires a voluntary sacrifice of their substance <note>original: "Subſtanz"; here referring to material wealth or physical possessions surrendered in ritual.</note> as the strongest testimony of their gratitude and affection toward him.

### Narada.

### Brahma.

### Narada.

### Brahma.

It is true, the human mind is stronger than an elephant—which men have nonetheless found the means to tame, even though they have never been able to completely conquer their own inclinations. Yet, the instrument of restraint for the mind is true wisdom, which brings to light the vanity of all human things.

<note>The comparison of the restless mind to a wild elephant is a classic image in Indian philosophy (particularly in the Upanishads and Buddhist texts), symbolizing a powerful force that must be disciplined through spiritual practice.</note>

## Narada

O Father! You say that God is only One. And yet it is said that *Ram* <note>Rama, one of the primary avatars of the god Vishnu</note>, whom we are taught to call God, was born in the house of *Dschesfarit* <note>likely a phonetic rendering of Dasharatha, Rama’s father</note>; that *Chrischen* <note>Krishna, another major avatar of Vishnu</note>, whom we call God, was born in the house of *Basdeo* <note>Vasudeva, the father of Krishna</note>; and so many others besides. How are we to unravel this mystery?

## Brahma

You must regard these as special revelations of God for certain great purposes; as, for example, in the case of the 1600 <note>Traditional Sanskrit texts usually cite the number of Gopis or wives as 16,000; the transcription here may reflect a specific regional variant or a clerical error.</note> women called *Gapi* <note>Gopis; in Hindu tradition, these are the cowherd women devoted to Krishna</note>, when all the men of *Sirendap* <note>possibly a corruption of a regional kingdom name</note> were destroyed in war. These women prayed for husbands, and their request was granted to them in a single night, and they became pregnant. But you must not think that God, who is introduced in this story as the actor <note>original: "Thäter"; meaning the one who performed the deed</note>, is subject to human passions or weaknesses. He is pure in Himself and, moreover, incorporeal. In the same way, He appears in a thousand forms at once, and is called by a thousand names. He assumes a thousand shapes without changing His original nature in the slightest.

<summary>Brahma explains the concept of divine avatars, clarifying that although God is one and incorporeal, He takes on various physical forms and names to fulfill specific divine purposes on Earth.</summary>

\*) In the Parsi religion, the Amesha Spentas are the seven primary heavenly spirits who, according to the Revelation of John <note>The author is drawing a comparative link between Zoroastrianism and the Christian Book of Revelation (specifically the "seven spirits before the throne"), a common practice in 18th and 19th-century scholarship.</note>, stand before the throne of God—protective archetypes of everything immortal, excellent, and glorious.

\*\*) Behesht is an ancient Persian word and means excellent or glorious—the heaven of the chosen and the angels of God.

### 5.
## To Ormuzd.

To think purely, to speak purely, to act purely; to do and fulfill this, and to learn to do it—that is what I myself learn, and what I teach to mankind. For this, Ormuzd, grant me fortune! <note>The triad of "Good Thoughts, Good Words, Good Deeds" (Humata, Huxta, Huvarshta) is the foundational ethical maxim of Zoroastrianism.</note>

To those pure and holy of heart, of word, and of deed, to him who performs works worthy of Behescht <note>original: "Behescht" (Garödmāna), the highest heaven or "Abode of Song."</note>, grant double fortune!

# Hymn

In the name of Him whose name is a refuge,
Whose praise is the ornament of eloquent tongues.
The Highest, the One, all-knowing, eternal,
Who grants power to the weak, to the abandoned,

He adorned the heavens with hosts of stars,
And decorated the earth with humans, as if with stars;
He arched the vault of the rolling sphere,
And raised up the four elements <note>The classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire, which were believed to compose all physical matter.</note>.

He gives fragrance to the rosebud's bosom,
And crowns the mother-bush with flower-children.
He weaves the bridal gown for Spring's brides <note>A common metaphor in Persian poetry where the blossoming of flowers in spring is likened to a wedding procession.</note>.
And teaches the cypress at the lakeside
To lift its charming, its beautiful head.

With success He crowns the good intention,
And humbles the pride of self-arrogance.
He watches at midnight by the solitary man’s lamp,
And passes the day with the children of sorrow.

From His sea arises the spring cloud,
Which waters the roses and the thorn alike.
From His garden blows the autumn breeze,

Should He veil His face, the mighty spheres
Of the great lights <note>A reference to the celestial bodies, such as the sun, moon, and planets, which were thought to move in crystalline spheres.</note> would quickly sink into nothingness.

From the heavenly vault down to the deep abyss,
Whichever way we direct our senses and thoughts:
Whether we hasten upward or descend,
There is no grain of dust that His power does not fill.

Wisdom is confounded by His essence;
To search out His ways is beyond human power.
The angels blush because they cannot grasp Him,
The heavens marvel that they are in motion.

### 15.
## Ossian to the Moon. <note>Ossian was a legendary Gaelic bard. These poems, published by James Macpherson in the 1760s, were hugely influential in the Romantic movement and often focused on the melancholy beauty of nature.</note>

Daughter of heaven, you are beautiful!
The silence of your countenance is kindness.
You step forth in lovely strides.
The stars in the east await your blue step. <note>original: "blauen Tritt" — A poetic reference to the moon's path across the deep blue of the night sky.</note>
The clouds rejoice when you come, oh moon!
And their dark edges stand gilded.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who is like you in the sky?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Daughter of the night!
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The stars blush when you look forth,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Quickly they turn away their sparkling eye!

And where do you hide yourself from your course,

# 16.

## Ossian to the Evening Star.

Star of the descending night!
Fair is thy light in the west.
Thou liftest thy unshorn head <note>original: "ungeschornes Haupt" — A poetic way of describing the star's rays as long, uncut hair, a common image in Ossianic poetry influenced by classical Greek epithets.</note>
From thy cloud
And stately is thy step upon thy hill.

At what lookest thou upon the plains?
The stormy winds are laid:
The murmur of the stream comes from afar:
Roaring waves climb the distant rock:
The evening gnats are on their feeble
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; wings;
And in the field is the humming of their flight.

At what lookest thou, fair light?
But thou smilest and departest.
The waves surround thee with joy
And bathe thy lovely hair.
Farewell, thou silent beam!

### 2.
# Song of Abulata elsindi <note>original: "Abulata elsindi" — Refers to Abu 'l-'Ata' al-Sindi, a famous 8th-century poet of the Umayyad and Abbasid eras who was of Sindhi (Indian) origin but wrote in Arabic.</note>

# Song of Ta'abbata Sharran <note>original: "Taabbat Schorra." Ta'abbata Sharran (meaning "He who has carried a mischief under his arm") was a famous 6th-century "brigand poet" of the pre-Islamic era, known for his prowess in desert survival and warfare.</note>
->from the Arabic.<-

## Occasion.

The poet had fallen in love with a girl. She promised to marry him, but after some time she took back her word because she had been frightened by others that, as the wife of such a bold warrior, she would soon become a widow.

They say to her: do not take him!
He is a victim to the first sword-point he encounters.
She does not know what she should do, because she fears
The beloved wanderer of the night <note>This likely refers to the poet's reputation as a "Sa'luk" or brigand who moves through the desert by night.</note> will make her a widow.
Sleep rarely creeps upon him; his business is blood vengeance
And that he meet the bronze-skinned warriors. —

### I.

We lived long in this spacious castle <note>original: "Burg." Given the geographic context, this refers to the fortified palace-complexes typical of ancient South Arabian civilizations like the Himyarites.</note>
->A life far from want and from lack.<-

->spear,<-

->Now in embroidered, now in green variegated dress.<-

->-<-

<margin>*) Hud is Eber. <note>original: "Hud ist Eber." In Islamic tradition, the prophet Hud is often identified with the biblical patriarch Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews and various Arabian tribes.</note></margin>
We served kings who were far from base-
   ness,
And were also irreconcilable toward deception
   and vice.
They showed us the way to happiness through Hud’s *) religion:
We believed in miracles, resurrection, and a bet-
   ter life.
Whenever an enemy invaded our lands,
Then we marched out together against him with
   sharpened spears;
We fought bravely against him for wife and child
Upon brown, fallow, red, and long-necked
   steeds.
We inflicted wounds on all who attacked us,
With our swords, until they were put to flight.

## II.

We lived long in this castle <note>original: "Burg." This refers to the massive stone fortifications and palaces (qasr) characteristic of the ancient Himyarite and Sabaean civilizations in southern Arabia.</note>, no worry
Tormented us, except for the land, which bore
   a rich harvest.
Each day, the evening brought back to us camels
By the hundreds, which at the watering place
   delighted our eyes,
And twice as many sheep, as beautiful
As white stags, and slow-trotting cows.

---

## 9.

# Traits from an Arabic Poem
# of Consolation.

### regarding the deceased mother of a
### hero.

We keep our swords and spears ready!
And yet fate kills us, even without an attack.
We keep swift steeds upon their feet;
And yet they do not snatch us away from
The malice of sudden misfortune.

<vocab>Castle, Deity, Arabic, Consolation poem, Hero, Swords, Spears, Fate, Steeds</vocab>

--- Page 165 ---
<meta>This page continues the translation of the Arabic elegy (poem of consolation) regarding the death of a hero's mother, picking up from the reflection on mortality and fate.</meta>

Who was it that never came to love the world?
And yet, no enjoyment of love is possible.
Your share of the beloved in this life
Is but a part of the dream-vision of the imagination.

May God’s mercy be the *Hanuth* <note>original: *Hanuth*. A fragrant powder used in traditional Arabic burial rites.</note> *)
Of the countenance, whose veil is beauty.
Even if her body decays within the belly of the earth,
To our memory, it remains fresh and new.

The carpet of honor is spread over you;
For your son’s dominion flourishes.
May your resting place be watered
By a rain from the morning clouds,
As gentle as your hand once was.

You have departed to a place
Where neither South nor North wind
Carries the sweet fragrance of incense to you,
Nor sprinkles you with any gentle coolness. —

Into a dwelling where every inhabitant is a stranger,
Eternally estranged from his homeland,
And his cords <note>The "cords" or "ropes" (*Strikke*) likely refer to the stays of a nomad's tent, symbolizing the final breaking of earthly ties and the end of the journey.</note> are torn asunder.

---

*) The fragrant scattering powder that the Arabs sprinkle upon the face of the dead: The veil here is the burial shroud of the deceased.

There dwells the chaste one, the well-protected,
Pure as the water in the clouds of heaven;
Reserved, truthful in conversation;
The physician of sorrows <note>A poetic reference to death as the final healer of earthly suffering.</note> has now healed her.

One of us buries the other,
Posterity walks upon the heads of their ancestors.
How many an eye, once kissed,
Is now filled with pebbles and sand!
How many have now closed their eyes,
Who never even blinked at any misfortune.
Take refuge, Sayf al-Dawla <note>original: *Seifeddaule*. The Hamdanid Emir of Aleppo (r. 945–967), a famous patron of the arts and warrior against the Byzantine Empire.</note>, in patience!
And could even mountains match your stature?
You have experienced much of time's changing fortunes;
Through every change, one courage always remained with you.

## II.
## An Ode by the Persian Poet
## Hafez. <note>Hafez (c. 1315–1390) was a celebrated Persian lyric poet. His "Divan" became widely known in Europe during the Enlightenment and Romantic periods.</note>

---

My lap is full of roses,
My head is clouded with wine,
My beloved yields to my every desire—
The monarch of the world is my slave today!

<summary>This page concludes an epic Ossianic celebration of military victory and shifts to a brief, hedonistic ode by the Persian poet Hafez, emphasizing themes of love, wine, and triumph.</summary>
<keywords>Ossian, Fingal, Selma, Morven, Hafez, Persian poetry, victory song, bards, drinking shell</keywords>

--- Page 169 ---
<meta>This page continues the translation of an ode by the Persian poet Hafez, which began on the previous page. The catchword "Von" appears in the middle of the text, likely referring to the lines discussing honor and sweetness.</meta>

Listen! Bring no light into our circle,
For the moon of my beloved’s cheeks
Is at its full radiance during this feast—
Do not light the incense
   In our banquet hall;
For my soul finds refreshment
   Only in the balsamic scent of her locks—
Speak no more of the sweetness of sugar and honey;
I wish only to taste the sweetness of her lips. —
Wine is permitted in our chambers;
Only without you, O slender, beautiful cypress <note>In Persian poetry, the cypress tree is a standard metaphor for the tall, graceful, and elegant stature of the beloved.</note>
Adorned with the finest nuances,
Is it forbidden—
If you are absent, and the burden of sorrow weighs
   upon me;
Then I sit lonely in the corner of my cell. <note>The "cell" (German: *Zelle*) likely refers to a Sufi dervish’s retreat, suggesting a blend of spiritual devotion and romantic longing.</note>
Why do you speak to me of honor?
It does not concern me—
Why do you speak my name?
It does not move me—
My ear listens only to the melody of the flute,
To the tones of the harp;
My eye is fixed only
Upon your crimson lips
And upon the cup as it goes around!
We love good wine to excess;
We are in love, and our eyes sparkle.

<vocab>Incense, locks, sugar, honey, cypress, crimson, banquet hall</vocab>

<summary>This page continues a lyrical ode by the Persian poet Hafez, celebrating the intoxication of love and wine while dismissing social honors and religious seclusion in favor of the beloved's presence.</summary>
<keywords>Hafez, Persian poetry, Sufism, wine, cypress metaphor, banquet, romantic devotion, dervish cell</keywords>

### A.

Boy! <note>German: *Knabe*. In the tradition of Persian poetry, the *Saki* (cupbearer) is often a young man who serves wine at a gathering, serving as a catalyst for both physical and spiritual intoxication.</note> bring the cups and fill them all with

->the sun!<- <note>A vivid metaphor where the radiant, golden wine is compared to the sun, and the round, silver or ceramic cup is compared to the moon that contains it.</note>

Pour out the liquid flames,

He wishes to carouse, whether it be permitted to him

## C.

I love a beauty. She is
Like the rose in the shade of the hyacinth bower;
Her ruby lips breathe the sweetest breath!
When she spreads the snare of her hair
Across her cheeks, she speaks to the Zephyr <note>The Zephyr is the gentle west wind, often personified in poetry as a messenger between lovers or a bringer of spring.</note>,
Keep our secret!
O beautiful and sweet are her cheeks.
O Heaven! grant the good woman an eternal life;
For eternal are her charms! —

When I began to love, I said:
Before I find this pearl of my desire,
A bottomless sea opens up richly before me —
And its waves will struggle with me.
Pour a drop of wine upon the ground!
This fate now belongs to the greatest heroes —
By comparison, the power of Jamshid <note>original: "Dschamschid." A legendary king of ancient Persia who possessed a magical cup that showed the entire world.</note>
And the strength of Kay Khosrow <note>original: "Rhei Chosru." A semi-legendary king of the Kayanian dynasty of Persia, celebrated in the Shahnameh.</note>
Are but vain fairy tales.

Do not deny me the sight of your stature,
Which resembles a cypress <note>In Persian literary tradition, the cypress tree is the standard metaphor for the tall, graceful, and elegant gait of the beloved.</note>,
I sit myself down by the spring of your fountain;
For so soft and pleasant is its water’s
Bubbling! —

If you wish to fetter me with your bonds,
O fetter me soon!
For misfortune follows delay,
The lover's sufferings are heavy! —

the deeds of the ancient kings of Persia. <note>This project became the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), one of the world's longest epic poems and the national epic of Greater Iran.</note> The Sultan had the poet summoned to him at once, flattered him, approved the plan for his work, and promised a rich reward once he had completed it. It is claimed that Ferdowsi worked for thirty years on this poem. Full of confidence, he presented a clean copy to his king after the work was finished. In the meantime, however, Mahmud had listened to the malicious representations of his Vizier, <term>Vizier: A high-ranking political advisor or minister.</term> who was Ferdowsi’s enemy, and deigned to give him little attention.

This famous unfortunate man had entirely neglected the care of his own fortune in favor of the elaboration of his work, and expected at least to be elevated to the rank of Emir. <term>Emir: A title of high rank, often denoting a prince, commander, or governor.</term> Through various small epigrams <note>original: "Epigrammen." Short, pithy, and often satirical poems.</note> which he allowed to fall into Mahmud’s hands, he sought to remind him of his promise. Among these was also this one:

> ->sea,<-
> ->Yet I have not found even a single pearl —<-

<meta>This page continues the biography of the Persian poet Ferdowsi. The previous page established that despite dedicating thirty years to the Shahnameh, Ferdowsi was denied his promised reward due to the intrigues of a jealous Vizier, leading the poet to express his disappointment through short, sharp poems.</meta>

L 2 18.

When the poet finally saw that all his effort was in vain, and that he could hope for nothing from an ungrateful court, he decided to leave it, after having devised a revenge that was as humorous as it was bitter. On the night before his departure, he gave the very favorite <note>original: "Günstling." Referring here to the King's influential advisor.</note> of the King—the one who had been hostile toward him—a sealed paper and told him that it contained a fable intended for Mahmud’s amusement. — At the same time, he asked him not to present it until he found that Mahmud was more sorrowful and pensive than usual due to burdensome affairs of state. When, two or three days later, the Vizier <term>Vizier: A high-ranking political minister or advisor to a Muslim monarch.</term> indeed found his master in the described state of mind, he presented the writing which, according to Ferdowsi's <note>The source spells the name "Ferdussi." He is the author of the Persian national epic, the *Shahnameh*.</note> claim, was meant to restore his natural cheerfulness. The King broke the seal and found the most biting satire. <note>This refers to the famous *Hajw-nama*, a scathing poem in which Ferdowsi mocks Sultan Mahmud’s character and low lineage.</note> The poet begins by dispassionately recounting Mahmud's promises, complains that they have not been fulfilled, and finally bursts out in the manner we have provided above.

<summary>Ferdowsi, realizing he will never be rewarded by the Sultan, flees the court after tricking his enemy into delivering a scathing satire to the King. This poem, disguised as a comforting fable, serves as the poet's final, bitter revenge against his ungrateful patron.</summary>

## Ninth Canto.

->(One from the Shepherd Chorus.)<-

### The Shepherd Chorus.

Yes, Love! your power is great, like the force of death,
And your glow like the wrath of the slayer; <note>original: "Zürnen des Würgers." The "slayer" or "strangler" likely refers to the personification of death or the grave.</note>
The flames of fire are not as ravenous as you!
The Creator himself fashioned this holy flame,
Which blazes in our breast. No flood
Can quench this fire in its passion; no stream
Can wash it away—Offer us, oh rich man, your house
Full of treasures; your gold and you yourself
Would be despised!

### The Punishment of the Disobedient.

<image-desc>decorative horizontal divider with a central knot design and stylized floral extensions</image-desc>

**U**nder the reign of Sultan Mahmud Subuktegin <note>Mahmud of Ghazni (971–1030), the prominent ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire.</note>, the governor of the city of Nisa in Khorasan <note>original: "Charesan" — a historical region in Central Asia, now spanning parts of Iran, Turkmenistan, and Afghanistan.</note> overthrew a very wealthy merchant and had him thrown into a prison. The merchant found the means to escape and made his way to Ghazni <note>original: "Gassim" — likely a transcription for Ghazni, the capital and seat of the Sultan's power.</note>, the capital and residence of the Sultan, where he threw himself at his feet and pleaded for justice. Sultan Mahmud issued a written order to the governor, commanding that he should restore the merchant to his previous standing regarding all his goods and assets. The governor received the letter, but in his thoughts—

The merchant, however, was not indifferent; he went repeatedly to Ghazni <note>original: "Gasnin" — the capital of the Ghaznavid Empire.</note>, took note of the time when the Sultan left his palace, and pleaded once more for justice against the unjust and cruel governor <note>original: "Statthalter"</note>. The governor was taken into custody and, with the Sultan’s letter in his hand, was hanged from the gallows, while the executioner cried out in a loud voice: "Behold, this is the punishment of those who are disobedient to their master!"

---

Sultan Mahmud Sabuktigin <note>original: "Subegtegin" — better known as Mahmud of Ghazni, who ruled from 998 to 1030 AD.</note> was the son of Sabuktigin, who before his accession to the throne had been a slave at the court of the Samanids <note>original: "Samaneer" — a Persianate dynasty that ruled over Central Asia and Greater Iran.</note>. He rose so quickly in rank and honor that he was finally even permitted to ascend the throne of Khorasan <note>original: "Chorasan" — a vast historical region encompassing parts of modern-day Iran, Afghanistan, and Turkmenistan.</note>. After his death, he was succeeded by Sultan Mahmud, who expanded the empire through great conquests in India. He ruled in the fourth century of the Islamic calendar <note>original: "muhammedanischen Zeitrechnung" — refers to the Hijri era.</note>, or in the 10th century according to the Christian era. His capital and residence was Ghazni <note>original: "Gasnin"</note> on the Indian border, which he preferred over the city of Bukhara <note>original: "Bochara"</note> in order to remain closer to the regions of his conquests.

### Caliph Mansur’s Vain Attempt to Convert a Christian

---

Caliph Mansur <note>Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. 754–775 AD), the second Abbasid Caliph and the primary founder of the city of Baghdad.</note> had a physician at his court who was a Christian and was named George, son of Bukhtishu <note>original: "Georg Sohn Bacht Jeschua" — Jurjis ibn Bukhtishu, a renowned Nestorian Christian physician from the Academy of Gondishapur.</note>. The prince loved this man immensely because he was successful in his cures <note>original: "glücklich in Curen"</note> and had even saved the Caliph himself from one of the most dangerous of illnesses. George, son of Bukhtishu, had already reached a venerable old age and now fell into a serious illness. The Caliph expressed a desire to see him and ordered that he be brought before his throne on his sickbed with the utmost care. The command was carried out, and the Caliph immediately asked about his well-being. The physician answered him and requested the favor of being sent back to his homeland, for before his

death he would like to speak once more with his loved ones, especially his only son, and also wished to rest in the grave with his fathers. —

The Caliph replied to him: "Physician, fear God! Become a Muslim <note>original: "Muselman"</note>, and you shall receive Paradise." The physician answered him: "In Paradise or in Hell, it matters not! If only I am with my fathers."

The famous historian Abulfaradsh <note>Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a prominent scholar and prelate of the Syriac Orthodox Church who wrote in Arabic and Syriac.</note>, who tells this little story, adds that the Caliph, after having received the physician's answer with a smiling face, used every effort to dissuade the man from his wish. But when he saw that he remained steadfast in his intention, he sent him back to his country with a gift of ten thousand gold florins <note>original: "Goldgulden"</note>. From this, one can conclude the great generosity <note>original: "Freigebigkeit"</note> of Caliph Mansur. The physician was at home in the city of Gondishapur in Persia. A eunuch <note>original: "Verschnittener"</note> was ordered to bring the sick man back there, and he indeed died in his native city.

## Hajjaj.

**H**ajjaj <note>Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf (661–714 AD), a famous and famously harsh governor of the Umayyad Caliphate.</note> was a governor of Arabia under the Caliphate of Abd al-Malik <note>reigned 685–705 AD</note>, the son of Marwan, from the house of the Umayyads. His cruelties and his thirst for power had made this governor hated everywhere. — Once, he encountered a dervish <note>A Muslim ascetic or monk known for their poverty and austerity.</note> in the region of Baghdad. He asked for the man's prayer. Immediately, the monk lifted his eyes toward heaven and prayed: "God! Take his soul!" Hajjaj was naturally not pleased with this prayer and called the dervish to account for it. The dervish answered: "That prayer is good for you and for all the faithful." <note>The implication being that death would stop Hajjaj from committing more sins and relieve the suffering of the people.</note>

---

Abulfaradsh <note>The historian Bar Hebraeus, previously mentioned.</note> calls the governor Hajjaj the son of Yusuf, and the author of the Rose Garden <note>The *Gulistan*, a landmark work of Persian literature by the poet Saadi Shirazi (1210–1291).</note> calls him simply Hajjaj Yusuf. One must also note that Abd al-Malik, the son of Marwan, ascended the Caliph's throne in the year 60 of the Flight <note>original: "Flucht." Refers to the Hijra, the migration of the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar.</note>.

## Extract from the History of the Persian Emperor Shapur.

During the minority of the Persian King Shapur <note>Shapur II, also known as Shapur the Great (reigned 309–379 AD). Legend states he was crowned in his mother's womb.</note>, son of Hormizd, Tair, a general of the Arabs, undertook a bloody war against the Persians, during which he had the capital of the empire plundered. —— He made the sister of the young Prince Shapur a slave and led her away with him. — When Shapur assumed the government, he attacked Tair and actually took him prisoner in a strong castle through the treachery of his sister <note>The text identifies her as Shapur's sister who was previously captured, though other historical traditions sometimes identify the woman who betrayed the fortress as Tair's daughter, al-Nadirah.</note>, who had opened the gate of the fortress. — Before he took full revenge on Tair, he first carried out a great massacre among the Arabs. After this had been driven with extreme heat for long enough, he decided to increase his cruelty by letting the unfortunate souls die under the most protracted tortures. He commanded that everyone who was captured should have their shoulders separated from their body. <note>This brutal practice led to Shapur's nickname in Arabic tradition: *Dhū al-Aktāf*, which translates to "He who pierces shoulders."</note> Malik, one of the ancestors of Muhammad, asked him how he could possibly have such courage to subject human beings to such cruel torments? Shapur answered: The astrologers have

Shapur is also written as *Sabur*, although the former spelling is the better one.

## Magnanimity of a Female Regent.

During the reign of Sultan Mahmud <note>Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998–1030), a powerful ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire</note>, Sebektegin Fakhr al-Dawla <note>original: *Sachr eddaulet*; referring to the Buyid amir Fakhr al-Dawla</note>, King of Isfahan, Rey, Qom, Kashan, and the province of Kohistan in Khorasan, passed away. He left as his successor Majd al-Dawla <note>original: *Madsched eddaulet*</note>, his son, who was still a minor. During his minority, his mother Sayyida <note>original: *Seida*; referring to Sayyida Shirin, a notable female ruler of the Buyid dynasty</note>, a lady of extraordinary wisdom, held the scepter. The entire populace congratulated themselves on her government. When the young prince reached his majority, because he was unfit to hold the rudder of state himself due to his dull intellectual faculties, he was permitted to keep the title of King, while his mother continued the government in his stead. — Sultan Mahmud, King of Transoxiana <note>original: *Maueralnahar*; from the Arabic *Mā Warāʾ al-Nahr*, "what is beyond the river"</note>, Turkestan, and a large part of Khorasan and India—whose eye was caught by the possession of such powerful states—dispatched an envoy to the lady. The envoy was required to pay her the "compliment" that she must respect the Sultan as her King. ## Where one should perform one’s prayer.

After Genghis Khan <note>original: *Dschenkischan*</note> had completed his great conquests on this side of the Oxus <note>The Amu Darya river, traditionally the boundary between the Persian world and Central Asia</note> and was about to return to Great Tartary, he was in Bukhara <note>original: *Bochara*; a major center of Islamic trade and scholarship in modern-day Uzbekistan</note> when he unexpectedly entered into a religious dispute with two Muslim <note>original: *Mohammedanischen*</note> doctors. He engaged in this debate all the more willingly because he was curious to hear their doctrine. The Muslim doctor who acted as the spokesman said to him: "The Muslims believe in a single God, Creator of Heaven and Earth, who has no equal." Genghis Khan replied: "I believe in Him as well."

## Tai and Sherik
### or
### Trust and Loyalty.

Before the divine Prophet <note>referring to Muhammad</note> enlightened his fatherland with the light of faith, the Arabs were idolaters <note>original: *Götzendiener*; literally "servants of idols," referring to the pre-Islamic period of polytheism in the Arabian Peninsula known as the Jahiliyyah.</note>. They worshipped a good and an evil god, and celebrated a special day of the week for each. The one day was considered lucky; and whoever appeared before the King on that day was granted his request without restriction. But whoever committed the imprudence of coming before the King’s throne on the unlucky day was brought without delay to the evil god as an expiatory sacrifice <note>original: *Sühnopfer*; a sacrifice offered to appease a deity or atone for a transgression.</note>.

The officer came running quickly to the Sultan with his plunder and presented it to him. "Place a chain around the robber's neck," said the Sultan; and turned to the peasant: "take him with you, he is your slave; sell him, or do with him as you please."

## The Merchant of Baghdad.

## Abdallah and Balsora.

The name Helim is even now famous throughout all eastern parts of the world. Among the Persians, to this very day, he is called Helim the Naturalist <note>original: Naturforscher. In this period, the term refers to a scholar of the natural world, encompassing biology, chemistry, and physics.</note>. For he knew all the powers of herbs, understood all the influences of the stars, and knew those secrets that were impressed upon the soul of Solomon, the son of David <note>A reference to the legendary wisdom and magical knowledge attributed to King Solomon in Middle Eastern traditions.</note>.

At the same time, Helim was the Governor of the Black Palace of the Kings of Persia, and the foremost physician to the Great King Alnareschin. Alnareschin was the most fearsome tyrant who had ever ruled in this land. Fearful, suspicious, and cruel, he had, out of unfounded suspicion, [executed] thirty-five of his

## The Power of Religion.

When the Caliph **Husseni** <note>Husayn ibn Ali (626–680 AD), the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and son of Ali ibn Abi Talib.</note>, a son of the great **Ali**, sat at table, one of his slaves let a bowl full of boiling rice fall upon his head. Angrily, the Caliph looked at the slave, and the latter, trembling and shaking, threw himself down at his feet and spoke the following words from the **Quran**: *Paradise is prepared for those who restrain their anger and master it.* <note>The slave is quoting from the Quran, Surah Ali 'Imran (3:134), which extols the virtues of self-control and forgiveness.</note> Coldly, Husseni answered: "I am not angry." The slave continued with the same verse: *And those who forgive those who have offended them.* Husseni, without looking at him: "I forgive you." The slave spoke further: *And God loves above all those who repay evil with good.* Husseni kindly reached out his hand to him. "Well then! arise: I grant you your freedom and four hundred <term>silver drachmas</term> <note>original: *Drachmen Silbers*. While the drachma is Greek in origin, the term was often used in European literature to describe historical Middle Eastern currencies like the dirham.</note>." Moved, the slave embraced his feet and cried out: "Most magnanimous Lord! You resemble the noblest tree: it lends its shade, it gives its fruit even to him who, with a bold arm, hurls stones against it."

## 2.

An Arab was lost in the desert. For two days he found nothing to eat and was in danger of dying of hunger, until he finally came across one of the water pits <note>These were likely cisterns or wells dug along caravan routes.</note> from which travelers water their camels. There he saw a small leather bag lying on the sand. "God be praised," he said as he picked it up and felt it, "these are, I believe, dates or nuts; how I shall refresh and sustain myself with them!" In this sweet hope, he opened the bag, saw what it contained, and cried out in great sadness: "Alas! They are only pearls." <note>This is a classic Eastern parable illustrating that the value of objects is relative to one’s needs; in the desert, food is more precious than gems.</note>

### 6.

A Greek doctor had agreed with a patient for a certain sum of money that he would cure him of his tertian fever <note>original: "dreitägigen Fieber"; a fever that recurs every third day, historically a common symptom of malaria.</note>. But instead of curing him, he gave him such remedies that changed the tertian fever into a semi-tertian one. The parents of the patient dismissed the doctor entirely, as he understood his business so poorly. He said to them: "Then pay me half of the promised money, for I have indeed driven away half of the illness."

### 7.

An Egyptian lady sent for a famous astrologer and asked him to discover the cause of her unrest <note>original: "Gemüthsunruhe," referring to an inner state of anxiety or spiritual agitation.</note>. Based on the position of the heavens at that time, the astrologer drew up a chart and delivered a long discourse upon it, which finally exhausted the lady completely. At last he fell silent, and the lady handed him a drachma <note>A silver coin of ancient Greece, used here likely as a generic term for a small payment.</note>. The astrologer was not satisfied with this and said: he could also see from the chart he had drawn that the lady was not exactly rich. "That is quite true," she replied. The astrologer continued to study his chart and asked: "Have you lost nothing?" She answered: "I have lost that which I just gave to you."

### 12.

A man wrote to his father from a foreign land saying that a severe illness had overcome him, from which, praise God, he had now recovered; however, he could assure him of this much: that another person would not have survived it. The father gave him a cold-blooded reply: "My son, you can believe me—if you had died and plunged me into mourning, it would have been of such benefit to me that I would never have had to exchange another word with you again in my life."

He was given the advice to discover the culprit <term>Thäter: an older spelling of "Täter," meaning perpetrator or culprit</term> with the help of the Holy Gospel. <note>This likely refers to the historical practice of "bibliomancy" or "sortes sanctorum," where a Bible was used as a divination tool to identify criminals or predict the future.</note> He replied: "If the thief were obedient to the word of the Holy Gospel, he would not only have taken what is mine, but would also have killed me; for thus speaks our Lord: 'The thief comes only to steal and to murder.'" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 10:10. The man is sarcastically suggesting that if the thief actually followed the Bible's description of a thief, the situation would be much worse.</note>

## 14.

Thieves once broke into a house. It was night. They searched for something and found nothing. The master of the house came upon them and asked what they were searching for there? "You fools," he spoke, "you search for something in this house at night; how many things have I myself already searched for in here even by day and not found them!"

## 15.

A man who had worn himself out on his journey wept and said: "There is no poorer creature in the world than I." A burden-bearing donkey said to him: "O wise one, why do you sigh so bitterly over your fate? Go and thank God that you are not a donkey." *)

## 16.

A man who had a wicked wife complained that he had to endure as much hardship from her as the bottom millstone. <note>In a traditional grain mill, the bottom stone (the "bedstone") is stationary and bears the entire weight and friction of the rotating top stone.</note> He was answered: "Why does it vex you to be the bottom millstone by day, since you are the top one by night?" <note>A bawdy jest suggesting that while the man is "oppressed" or henpecked during the day, he takes the dominant position in bed at night.</note>

### 17.

Takas entrusted one of his servants with an important secret but commanded him to keep it hidden; he did so, but finally talkativeness overcame his tongue and he blurted it out. Takas ordered him to be beheaded; then one who was nearby spoke: "Do not kill this servant; you yourself are the cause of all this misfortune. First, keep the secrets of your own heart yourself, then you need not worry that another will scatter them. Trust your gemstones to those who have great treasures; but your heart’s secrets to no one but yourself."

### 18.

When a father saw that his son was getting teeth, he spoke sadly to his wife: "From where shall I get bread and side dishes <note>The original German "Zugemüse" refers to vegetables or other accompaniments served alongside a main portion of bread or meat.</note> for him?" — She answered him: "God, who creates the teeth, will also create bread for our child."

### 20.

**Lokman** <note>Lokman (or Luqman) is a legendary sage in Islamic tradition. Often described as an enslaved man of African origin, he is celebrated for his wisdom, which many scholars compare to that of Aesop.</note> had the misfortune of being black, thick, and fat. Now, a master had lost a slave, and when he saw **Lokman**, who resembled the missing man, he took him for that slave, had him seized, and kept him strictly at hard labor. After a full year, the actual slave arrived; the error was recognized and the master expressed regret. However, **Lokman** said with a smile: "Do not be troubled, friend! Your harshness has driven away my fat belly this year; for that, I owe you thanks—Moreover, I also have a slave whom I treated just as harshly as you treated me. But since I now know how difficult it was for me, I will no longer keep him so strictly in the future."

### 21.

A king in Damascus had the habit of wandering through the city every day at dawn to hear what the people said about him. One day, he came to a temple where he saw two poor monks <note>In the context of Damascus and this style of literature, these "monks" are likely Sufi dervishes—ascetics known for their poverty and spiritual devotion.</note>. One of them, believing he was not being heard by anyone, began: "If, on the Day of Judgment, the kings of this earth—who raise their heads so proudly and spend their time in joy and luxury—should enter heaven alongside us poor, oppressed ones, I think I would rather remain lying under my gravestone. And even if our own wise and just king came, I would still bash in his skull <note>original: "Hirnschale"</note> at the gates of paradise—" 

When the king heard this, he went home, summoned the monks, presented them with rich gifts, and showed them great honor. One of the monks asked him what they had done to deserve such great kindness from him. "So that you do not bash in my skull at the gates of paradise," was his answer.

### 24.

A traveler saw a lame fox that had neither front nor back legs. He marveled at this sight and could not understand how this lame, powerless animal could still nourish itself. While he was thinking this, a lion came who had a strong fox in its claws and ate half of it. The lame fox sated itself on the remains. The next day, a bird of prey dropped some of its catch right in front of this legless fox, which it then consumed. Now this man believed that, just as this animal was fed through God’s providence <note>original: "Gottes Fürsehung" — the theological concept that God provides for all living things.</note>, he might likewise count on it. After he had remained there for several days and was completely exhausted by hunger, he heard a voice: "Be gone, you lazy man, and become rather a predatory lion, than that you [should make] yourself into a lame fox—"

### The Wolf, the Hare, and the Fox.

**A** wolf was forced by hunger to leave the forest and lay in wait in the open field for humans. Just then, he was passing by a small hill and spotted a hare that was fast asleep and without a care. This was a lucky find for the greedy beast. He crept toward it as quietly as he possibly could. Nevertheless, the hare awoke from the wolf's snorting. The sound of the feet of the predator <term>predator|The original German uses "Räuber," literally "robber," a common historical term for a beast of prey.</term> may also have contributed to his fortunate awakening. The fearful creature attempted a leap to escape. But the wolf anticipated him and stopped him.

In this regard, he had dug a pit in the middle of his den and covered it with all kinds of brushwood, also including a secret exit within it, by means of which he could slip away secretly <note>original: "davon wischen könne"; literally "to wipe away," meaning to escape quickly and quietly</note> in case of need. —

At the very moment the hare departed from him, the fox immediately set the brushwood in such a way that he might achieve his goal.

Once he was prepared to flee through the hidden exit, he called out to the wolf and the hare, shouting in a loud voice: "My worthy guests, please, step inside!" But as soon as he heard them entering, he abandoned the den and made for the open fields. The hare and the wolf rushed into the fox’s den with all possible speed; however, the moment their feet touched the brushwood, they tumbled over one another down into the pit. The wolf, believing the hare had played this trick on him intentionally <note>original: "mit Fleis," meaning deliberately or with intent</note>, tore him to pieces, then leaped out of the pit and sought his fortune elsewhere.

---

### Moral.

A wise person neglects nothing that might protect them against deception, and through such vigilance, they are never caught off guard by a sudden attack.

# The Monkeys and the Bears.

A great number of monkeys lived in a very pleasant region filled with all kinds of fruit. A bear happened to travel through this wealthy area by chance. When he perceived the beauty of the place, along with the contented life of the monkeys, he said to himself: "It is surely unjust that these small creatures are so fortunate, while I, by contrast, must seek my sustenance with such great difficulty in the forests and upon the mountains." Immediately, he fell upon the monkeys and tore several of them to pieces in the fury of his wrath. However, the others all swarmed together and—because there was a great number of them—treated him very roughly. He was barely able to escape with his life.

When his audacity <note>original: "Verwegenheit," implying a reckless or insolent boldness</note> had been punished in this manner, he retreated to a mountain and let out such a mighty roar that an entire troop of bears gathered before him, to whom he recounted his experience. They laughed at him soundly. "Oh, you miserable fool <note>original: "Tropf," a term for a pitiable or simple person</note>," they said, "why do you allow yourself to be hunted and overcome by such small animals? ...slight change, **Babun**. In Arabic-Persian script, M and B are two letters that can easily be confused with one another. ## The Duck and the Moon.

On a moonlit night, a duck saw the reflection of the moon in the water and took it for a fish. She immediately dove down to catch it, but was deceived. She repeated this often, naturally always with unfortunate results. Finally, she grew weary of the game and let the fish be fish <note>original: "ließ den Fisch, Fisch sein" — a German idiom meaning to give up on a matter or leave it alone</note>. On the following nights, when the moon no longer shone, the duck saw real fish. However, because she imagined they were once again nothing but mere illusions, she did not desire to catch any. "I have already been deceived so many times," she said to herself, "I will not concern myself with them." In the meantime, amidst such fine imaginings, she had to die of hunger because she no longer wanted to catch any fish.

### The Raven, the Snake, and the Fox.

A raven had chosen the slope <note>original: "Abschuß" — referring to a steep incline or precipice of a mountain</note> of a mountain as his residence and had built his nest there in a crevice of the rock. However, a snake from the neighborhood was so malicious that she devoured the raven's young as often as he had any. This act of violence pierced the raven’s heart; he grieved bitterly over his many losses and finally resolved to seek revenge. To this end, he pondered a suitable means. But before he undertook anything, he revealed his thoughts to a fox in the neighborhood, as if to an old, dear friend. After recounting the causes of his frustration, he said: "My intention is to lie in wait for the time when the snake is asleep, and then to peck out her eyes so that she can no longer see my young, and I will have nothing more to fear from her."

### The Prodigal Mouse

A farmer <note>original: "Landmann"</note>, who looked ahead to future times, once locked up a great deal of grain in a barn after a bountiful harvest, with the intention of not opening it until a time of scarcity <term>Theurung: a historical term for a period of high prices and food shortage, often preceding a famine</term> occurred. For this reason, he also hid the key in a place that no one knew.

It happened by chance that a hungry mouse, whose hole was near the grain magazine <note>original: "Kornmagazine" — a storage facility</note>, began to gnaw through the wood and worked with her sharp teeth until she sensed that several grains of corn were falling from the barn through the bitten-out opening and into her hole.

This stroke of luck delighted her immensely; she considered it a gift from heaven, but because of this discovery she became so arrogant <note>original: "hochmüthig"</note> that from that moment on she considered herself the equal of Pharaoh <note>The mouse compares her sudden wealth to the legendary storehouses of the Egyptian Pharaohs</note>. The rumor of her good fortune spread—

### Moral.

In such a manner, most friends are usually accustomed to act. They visit you diligently as long as your table is set. Should you become poor once more, they abandon you.

## The Fox and the Drum.

A hungry fox crept back and forth in the forest, seeking something to snatch up. In this endeavor, he happened to come near a tree from which a drum hung; a branch touched the drum from time to time, moved by the force of the wind, thereby causing a sound. The fox did not spring at him immediately because he was not close enough; instead, he lay down behind a bush to wait for the right moment <note>original: "das Tempo" — here meaning the precise timing or opportune moment</note> when the rooster could no longer escape him. # The Shorebird and the Sea.

Two shorebirds <note>original: "Strandvögel" — likely referring to a species of plover or sandpiper</note> had their nest by the sea. When the female sensed it was her time to lay eggs, she said to the male: "Do look for a suitable place for the nest, so that we have neither burden nor danger to fear." "The place where we are now <note>original: "jezzo" — an archaic form of "jetzt," meaning "now"</note> is suitable enough," replied the male. "It is so pleasant <note>original: "lustig" — in this historical context, it means delightful or cheerful rather than funny</note> and well-situated that we will not find its equal anywhere else. Therefore, it seems to me advisable not to leave it."

"You are not considering this properly," the female began again; "suppose the sea should throw up high waves and carry away our young? Would not the loss grieve us for the rest of our lives?" "Oh," replied the male, "you must never believe that the sea would be so bold as to declare war upon us. Much less will it, without cause, show us such insult and annoyance, and swallow our young. — I would certainly know how to avenge myself, should it happen! But your worry, little wife! is entirely groundless. It is impossible that this

# Seventh Vein

# Heomo Berekehe <note>Likely a phonetic transcription of an Oriental name or title, possibly related to the "Humayun-nama" or a similar collection of Eastern wisdom and tales.</note>
## Memoirs.

### Chivalry of the Orient.

The order of knights-errant <term>knights-errant: wandering knights who traveled in search of adventure to prove their chivalric virtues</term> has always been too closely allied with sorcery for this subject not to deserve further observation over many other matters. — A people’s unique way of thinking and their customs can be discovered just as easily in their poems and romances as in their serious writings. For a poet of true genius, even if he grants his heroes greater perfection and fewer flaws than can be found in the imperfect nature of man, will nonetheless always depict the actual manners and morals, belonging either to his own or to preceding times. —

Esfendiar <note>Also known as Esfandiyar, a legendary prince and tragic hero from the Persian epic, the *Shahnameh*</note> was one of the most famous heroes in ancient Persia. Arjasp, son of Afrasiab, King of Turan (Scythia), was challenged, contested, and killed by him. — However, when he was sent by his father against the famous knight Rustem <note>Rostam, the most celebrated hero in Persian mythology, known for his extraordinary strength</note>, he was killed after a two-day duel by a blow with Rustem’s scepter <note>original: "Scepter"; likely referring to a heavy mace, the traditional weapon of Persian paladins</note>. For Rustem had discovered that a magical remedy <note>original: "Zaubermittel"</note> made one invulnerable against sword, spear, and arrow. — Rustem had many duels with his own son, Sohrab, without knowing that it was he with whom he fought. In one of these encounters, he killed him. These heroes are armored, wear plumed helmets, and carry spears, swords, scepters, shields, daggers, bows, and arrows. Their weaponry and the trappings of their horses are magnificent. The manner in which they attack one another appears exactly like the tournaments of the knights-errant <term>knights-errant: wandering knights of medieval romance who traveled to seek adventure and prove their chivalric virtues</term>. Only the circumstance that they also possess bows and arrows creates a distinction among them. —

# The Library of the King of India.

---

Dabschelim <note>King Dabshalim, a legendary Indian monarch frequently featured as the interlocutor in the fables of *Bidpai* (also known as *Kalila and Dimna*)</note>, King of India, possessed a library so vast that one hundred Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanen"; members of the highest Hindu caste, traditionally serving as priests and scholars</note> were required to maintain its order, and a thousand camels were needed to transport it. However, because he did not have the desire to read it in its entirety, he commissioned the Brahmins to extract the best and most useful material they could find and present it to him in the form of summaries. These learned men worked with such diligence that after twenty years had passed, they had compiled from the gathered excerpts a brief essence of all wisdom. This work consisted of two thousand volumes, which thirty camels could carry without much difficulty. They had the honor of presenting it to the King; but to their astonishment, they were told that he still found the load of thirty camels to be too heavy. Consequently, they reduced this load to fifteen, then to nine, then to four, and finally to two camels; indeed, in the end, only as much remained as a mule of average size could comfortably carry. ## On the Religion of the Kalmyks

The Kalmyks <note>A nomadic Mongolic people who migrated to the Caspian region</note> share their doctrine of faith—which is the so-called **Lamaist** religion <note>A form of Buddhism practiced in Tibet and Mongolia</note>—with their brothers, the Mongols, just as they largely share their script, language, and way of life. In this religion, as with the Indian faiths, one finds an entire doctrine regarding the structure of the universe and its past and future states, woven into a great framework of fables and illusions. Within it, one encounters the ancient doctrine of the **transmigration of souls** <term>transmigration of souls<gloss>The belief that after death, a soul is reborn in a new body, whether human or animal</gloss></term> in such an extensive sense that even all their deities (who were formerly human) were strictly subject to this law before their deification, and are said to have wandered through all kinds of animal bodies; at least, they believe this of many of their primary idols, or **Burchans** <term>Burchans<gloss>Derived from the word "Burqan," a Mongolian term for Buddha or a divine being</gloss></term>. It is remarkable that the Kalmyk-

<meta>This page continues the description of the Kalmyk (Kalmückisch) world-structure, picking up from the previous page's explanation of why the sun is said to contain glass. It transitions from the celestial bodies to the central axis of the universe and the arrangement of the worlds.</meta>

...because there are **burning glasses** <term>Brenngläser: magnifying lenses used to concentrate sunlight to start fires; the author uses this to justify why the Kalmyks believe the sun is made of glass</term>, which consequently must have been known in the Orient for a long time. They assume the moon is somewhat smaller than the sun and believe it consists of glass and water. The number of stars is fixed by them at ten thousand million—a figure over which **astronomers** <note>original: "Sternkündiger"</note> may debate among themselves. 

— In the Kalmyk **world-structure** <note>original: "Weltgebäude" — referring to their cosmological model</note>, the sun follows a circuit around the great central pillar or axis, **Siumer Sula** <note>The Kalmyk name for Mount Sumeru, the sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Buddhist cosmology</note>. This pillar, however, shows us four sides of different colors: a silver side, a sky-blue side, a golden side, and a dark red side. When the sun casts its rays upon the silver side, morning dawns; as the blue side is gradually illuminated, it moves toward midday; when it is perfectly noon, the sun shines upon the golden side; and when it finally turns toward the red, the evening glow arises, until the sun hides from our eyes behind the pillar and, consequently, it becomes night.

Around this pillar hover four large worlds in total, and between them, in pairs, are the smaller ones, of which there are consequently eight. Among the larger ones, they say, our world stands to the right and is called by them **Sambu-tup** <note>original: "Sambu-tup" — a variation of Jambudvipa, which in Buddhist cosmology is the "southern continent" where humans live</note>, because

Concerning the dwellings of the various **Burchans** <term>Burchan: a Mongolian and Kalmyk term for a Buddha or a high deity</term>, nothing more definite can be said than that they have been assigned to them partly in other regions of the Kalmyk world-structure and heavenly space. Countless others have been assigned dwelling places in the upper firmament, or heaven, to which a golden path leads across a high mountain. Atop this mountain floats a cloud that appears to consist of jasper, upon which a dwelling place has been assigned to the air spirit Adaboshi. At the foot of the mountain, a multitude of foxes reside; they attack the wicked souls and must keep them away from these blissful dwellings, which are the most distinguished paradise. Beneath the golden path, there is also a silver one leading toward the rising of the sun to that particular dwelling place where Abida Burchan <note>Amitābha Buddha, the Buddha of Infinite Light, who presides over the Pure Land or "Western Paradise"</note> enjoys a state of perfect rest. Then follows a copper path to the dwellings of the thirty-three benevolent air spirits—to be mentioned shortly—among whom the paradise for the not very meritorious and for childish souls is said to be located.

## Something on Natural Magic.

Among the many diverse arts that human ingenuity has devised, there are many that, upon first consideration, appear supernatural or at least miraculous. The ancient <term>Easterners</term> <note>original: "Morgenländer," literally "people of the morning land," a common historical term for the peoples of the Orient or Near East.</note> used to call such miraculous skills "magic arts," and they gave those who practiced these skills—and kept them secret from the uninitiated—the names of sorcerers, <term>necromancers</term> <note>original: "Schwarzkünstler," literally "black-artists."</note>, or <term>masters of a thousand arts</term> <note>original: "Tausendkünstler"; a term for a versatile entertainer, magician, or someone capable of many clever tricks.</note>

<meta>This page follows the conclusion of the description regarding the "Rausa-Nischin" and the Persian winter festival. The previous page ended with the warning that the festive beggar would be beaten if he did not clear the streets, signaling that the ritual was over.</meta>

over. Our current age is beyond such lofty ideas—an age in which the human spirit has attained greater maturity, and where the growth of <term>reason</term> <note>original: "Vernunft"; the author is reflecting Enlightenment values, where logical reasoning was seen as a way to temper the "overheated" imagination of earlier eras.</note> increasingly cools the heat of the imagination. We now believe little in the supernatural, and whatever can be explained entirely through natural forces is struck out from the records of the miraculous. We recognize no magic in the sense of the ancients, but rather a **natural magic**.

Most arts of the latter sort are arts of pleasure and curiosity; few possess at the same time an established utility. Among these undoubtedly useful arts belongs the so-called *Art of Deciphering* <note>original Latin: "Ars Decifratoria"; the study of cryptography and breaking codes.</note>, which, incidentally, also provides much enjoyment. A very brief system of this art deserves a place here before many other subjects, all the more so because this art—like all other arts—originally stems from the <term>Orient</term> <note>historical term for the East, specifically the Middle East and surrounding regions.</note> and was first cultivated by Eastern peoples. One of the most distinguished treatises on the nature, methodology, and utility of this art was composed in the 10th century by an Arab named *Abdallah ben Mahommed Nassir eddin altabori*.
