# First lines of the art of deciphering, or the Art of Deciphering or Decoding <note>original Latin: "Primae lineae artis decifratoriae"; the author uses both a Latin academic title and its German equivalent.</note>.

---

->§. 1.<-

The <term>art of deciphering</term> <note>original: "Entziferungskunst"; the skill of breaking codes without the original key.</note> teaches how to solve and read secret writings which are written not with ordinary characters, but with unknown ones. Such writings bear a resemblance to the hieroglyphs of the Egyptians, and thus the art of deciphering them bears a resemblance to the resolution and development of those hieroglyphs, which were the exclusive property of the priests. The invention of the art of deciphering is undoubtedly owed to curiosity and inquisitiveness, but it appears to be ancient. *)

> *) Some have said that Daniel already understood the art of decoding because he was the only one who could read and interpret the writing: *Numbered, Numbered, Weighed, and Divided* <note>original: "Mene, Mene, tekkel ufarsim"; these are the Aramaic words from the biblical Book of Daniel (5:25), appearing on the wall during Belshazzar's feast. The author considers it "ridiculous" to call this cryptography because it was a divine miracle, not a human linguistic skill.</note>. However, this is ridiculous.

<note>Vocabulary from the original page: Art of Deciphering, Art of Decoding, Hieroglyphs, Egyptians, Daniel, Numbered Numbered Weighed and Divided.</note>

<summary>This page defines the art of deciphering as the study of secret or unknown scripts, comparing it to the study of Egyptian hieroglyphs. It also dismisses the biblical story of Daniel as the origin of the craft, preferring a secular, historical view.</summary>
<keywords>cryptography, deciphering, hieroglyphs, Egyptian priests, Prophet Daniel, secret writing, history of science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the art of deciphering, moving from the historical origins mentioned on page 353 to the classification of secret writings and the theoretical requirements for decoding them.</meta>

### §. 2.

There are various types of secret writing that can all be addressed; *) here we are dealing with those secret writings which consist of a sequence of signs, each of which represents a single letter.

->*) e.g., Hieroglyphs or picture-writing.<-
-><term>Tachygraphy</term> <note>original: "Tachügrafi"; while this modernly refers to shorthand, the author defines it here as a system where every word has a specific sign.</note>, i.e., where every word<-
->has a sign, and so forth.<-

### §. 3.

The rules by which one deciphers such writings made with foreign characters are grounded in the nature of the language in which something has been expressed through arbitrarily chosen <term>ciphers</term> <note>original: "Zifern"; here meaning the symbols or signs used in the secret code.</note>. The complete set of rules used for deciphering is called the **science of deciphering**; and the application of these rules is the **art of deciphering**.

### §. 4.

The diversity of the languages in which secret writings are written creates a diversity of rules. However, in and of itself, the deciphering of a script written with unknown letters remains possible for all languages, provided one knows the **spirit of the language** <note>original: "Genius der Sprache"; this refers to the unique grammatical, phonetic, and structural patterns that characterize a specific language.</note> in which the secret writing is composed, and proceeds according to those rules of deciphering which are based on this spirit or the nature of the language.

### §. 5.

Anyone who wishes to decipher something must, therefore, understand the language in which the secret writing is composed. The more perfectly one knows a language in its full extent, the more successful they will be in deciphering secret writing within it. Not only is a knowledge of the language required for deciphering, but also an open mind or a particularly lively <term>genius</term> <note>original: "Genie"; in this context, it refers to natural talent, intellectual sharpness, and the innate ability to recognize patterns.</note>. Someone who is slow to grasp a matter will not get far in deciphering, and their work will not bring them pleasure, but will instead become extremely burdensome.

*) A true simpleton <note>original: "Dumkopf"; a blunt term used here to emphasize that deciphering is an intellectual discipline requiring sharp wits.</note> would do better to stay away from deciphering altogether. For such a person and the art of deciphering are a contradiction in terms.

### §. 6.

Patience is also sometimes necessary for deciphering, especially when the writings are very convoluted or too small. And a beginner, in particular, must have learned patience. Quiet and solitude also greatly aid deciphering, as they distance the decipherer from other thoughts. A more experienced person will eventually be able to decipher amidst the loudest noise.

### §. 7.

Beginners must, in order to make the task easier for themselves, choose large scripts for practice in deciphering. For the larger the script, the easier the decipherment. The larger a script is, the more opportunity one finds to apply the rules of the <term>art of deciphering</term> <note>original: "Entziferungskunst"; the systematic study and methodology of breaking codes or reading difficult handwriting.</note> and to make attempts; with small scripts, however, the rules of the art often cannot be applied sufficiently or properly.

### §. 8.

The work is easier if one knows in what language a writing is composed than if this is initially unknown. If the language is known, one also immediately knows what <term>special rules</term> <note>original: "Specialregeln"; specific linguistic patterns, such as letter frequency or common prefixes/suffixes, unique to a particular tongue.</note> must be applied, which are based on the nature of that language. If the language is unknown, one must first make various futile attempts, for which no rules can be given. One must then determine the language from certain infallible characteristics; for every language has its own external as well as internal peculiarities. —

### §. 11.

Once one has counted all the signs of a <term>secret writing</term> <note>original: "geheimen Schrift"; referring to a cipher.</note> and knows how often each one occurs, one proceeds further. 

In every language, certain letters occur more frequently than others; these one must also know. For example: in German, among all <term>auxiliary sounds</term> <note>original: "Hülfslaute"; a historical term for vowels.</note>, **e** occurs most often, unless it is in a very short text; among all <term>main sounds</term> <note>original: "Hauptlaute"; a historical term for consonants.</note>, the **n** [is most frequent]. Across all letters in general, it is the **e**.

Thus follows the second general rule:

> "That sign of a secret writing which occurs most often is generally to be taken for that letter which occurs most often in the language from which one is <term>deciphering</term> <note>original: "entzifert"</note>; and that sign which, next to this one, is present more frequently than the others, [is to be taken] for that letter which follows the most frequent one in that language. Thus, in German, the most frequent sign is generally to be assumed as **e**; that which [follows]...

### §. 12.

> "Once one has probably figured out one or two letters, one begins to compare the occurring words with one another and, for the time being, resorts to guessing. Through this, one will soon guess this or that word, and once one or two words are out, the rest will present little difficulty; and one will gradually discover all the letters and thus be able to read the entire script."

This is the third general rule, which can only be applied without hindrance when the foreign script has <term>word divisions</term> <note>original: "Abtheilungen der Wörter"; this refers to the use of spaces or marks to separate words, which was not always present in historical ciphers.</note>. If, however, it has no word division, the investigation proceeds slowly. Regardless of how the script is structured, it can be deciphered by applying the said rules, if one only takes the following special rules as an aid to the three general rules.

conclusions or make guesses based upon it." 
In German, the letters **b**, **d**, **f**, **ch**, **h**, **l**, **m**, **n**, **r**, **s**, and **t** 
occur most frequently.

### §. 22.

> X.) "The <term>decipherer</term> <note>original: "Entziferer."</note> must also, to facilitate his entire work, take note of those symbols that prefer to stand next to one another; that is, he must know which letters in a language love the neighborhood of others above all."

In German, **n** likes to follow **e**, and **e** likes to follow **n**. <note>The "en" and "ne" combinations are extremely common in German due to plural endings and verb conjugations.</note> **h** likes to follow **c**, and **ch** likes to follow **s**. <note>Referring to the common clusters "ch" and "sch."</note> **t** likes to follow **c**. **r** likes to follow **e**.

After a double **b**, no <term>consonant</term> <note>original: "Hauptlaut"; literally "main sound."</note> follows more frequently than **r**. <note>For example, in words like *Abbruch* (breakdown) or *Sabbath*.</note>

After **ff**, **t** commonly follows, unless a <term>vowel</term> <note>original: "Hülfslaut"; literally "auxiliary sound."</note> is present.

After **nn**, among the <term>consonants</term>, **t** is common. <note>Found in words like *kennt* (knows) or *rennt* (runs).</note>

### §. 24.

If the words in a secret script are not separated, then the deciphering is difficult, but it can still be done; if one only knows the rules of the <term>art of deciphering</term> <note>original: "Entziferungskunst"; early cryptanalysis</note> and knows the language. If the script is German, one knows, of course, that the most frequently occurring <term>cipher</term> <note>original: "Ziefer"</note> is **e**; that the one following it in frequency is an **n**; that an **n** likes to follow an **e**; and that words frequently end in **-en**. Thus one also knows how to look for the **ch**; one also soon recognizes **und** <note>"and"</note> and similar all-too-frequently occurring words if one is only attentive; and so forth. Thus there are aids enough to bring out the script, unless it were all too small; and even then, the task is not insurmountable <note>original: "unbesteiglich," literally "un-climbable"</note>.

If a secret script uses foreign symbols, and among them some are placed superfluously, then the <term>decipherment</term> <note>original: "Entziferung"</note> is indeed difficult, but still possible, as the superfluous or <term>null characters</term> <note>original: "nichts geltenden Buchstaben"; literally "non-valid letters," these are meaningless characters used to confuse the cryptanalyst</note> can be discovered, because they must appear according to certain rules if the person who is meant to know the secret is to be able to read the script. ->§. 27.<-

If a **secret script** <note>original: "geheime Schrift"</note> uses foreign symbols and, on top of that, has its words broken apart irregularly, it is treated in a similar way as if no **word division** <note>original: "Wortabtheilung"</note> were present at all. One therefore does well to rewrite such a script—which an expert in the language will soon identify as such—into a script without any divisions, and then **decipher** <note>original: "entzifert"</note> it according to the rules.

->§. 28.<-

Scripts that must be read from back to front, such as **Hebrew** <note>original: "Ebräische"</note>, are easily recognized by certain characteristics. In German, for example:

1. When, after identifying the letter *e*, another character frequently stands *before* this *e*, especially at the beginning of words; for very few words begin with *ne*, whereas many end with *en*. <note>The author is explaining how to detect reversed text: a common suffix like "-en" would appear as a prefix "ne-" if the word is written backwards.</note>

2. When, after finding a suspected *ch*, one finds that the first character <note>the letter 'c'</note> never or rarely appears alone, while the second <note>the letter 'h'</note> often appears without the other.

3. When words often begin with the symbol of the suspected *ch*. <note>In German, many words end with the letters "-ch" (such as *ich*, *auch*, or *doch*). If these symbols appear at the start of words in a cipher, it suggests the text is written in reverse.</note>

### §. 29.

We have stated above that one must first investigate the language in which an unknown script is composed. If one is intimately familiar with other languages besides German, it is easy to recognize in what language a **cipher script** <note>original: "Ziferſchrift"</note> is written; for every language has its own unique characteristics even when hidden in cipher. For example, the **Latin language** <note>original: "lateiniſche Sprache"</note> has very few double letters, especially at the end of words; on the other hand, it has many **monograms, bigrams, and trigrams** <note>referring to words of one, two, and three letters in length.</note>. **French** <note>original: "Franzöſiſche"</note> has many monograms and other small words, and also very rarely uses double letters.

<meta>This page continues the author's meteorological observations in the Middle East, shifting from the visibility of stars discussed on the previous page to the characteristics and physical effects of regional winds in cities like Aleppo and Basra.</meta>

The effect of the wind in the Arabian cities is also very diverse, according to the character of the surrounding regions. In Aleppo <note>original: "Haleb," the historic city in northern Syria.</note>, the west wind, which comes from the seaside, is humid, and the east wind from the desert is dry. On the island of Kharg <note>original: "Charadsj" or "Karek," an island in the Persian Gulf.</note> and in Basra, the southeast or sea wind commonly brought murky air, which was so humid that our table, when we ate outdoors in the evening, became damp in a short time. But it became dry just as quickly when the wind suddenly turned to the northwest. During the humid southeast wind, there is commonly a calm <note>original: "Windstille"; a lack of wind often associated with oppressive humidity in maritime climates.</note>—and thus a sweltering heat—on the island of Kharg and in Basra during the hottest time of year; the dry northwest wind, by contrast, is not so uncomfortable because the air is more in motion with it. However, it seems to be hotter (namely in the summer months—in winter it is colder). It makes all solid bodies such as wood, iron, etc. <term>etc.</term> <note>original: "2c.", an archaic abbreviation for "et cetera."</note>, even if they stand in the shade, as hot as if they were exposed to the sun's rays; even water in glass or metal pots becomes warm because of it. On the other hand, the water which was in <term>Gorgolats</term> or <term>Bardaks</term>, <gloss>that is, pots</gloss> <note>These are traditional porous earthenware vessels used throughout the Middle East to cool water through evaporation.</note>

Because the sun stands almost directly over Arabia during the summer solstice <note>original: "Sommerstillestande"</note>, it is so hot in most regions of this land that, unless out of the greatest necessity, almost no one sets out on a journey between eleven o'clock in the morning and three o'clock in the afternoon (during July and August). In Baghdad and on the island of Kharg <note>original: "Charedsj," an island in the Persian Gulf.</note>, and perhaps in other cities of this region as well, they sometimes sleep in a room beneath the house, into which they direct the wind from above through a kind of chimney, thereby setting the air in motion <note>The author is describing a *badgir* or wind-catcher, a traditional architectural element used to provide natural ventilation and cooling in hot climates.</note>. Since, however, a wind traveling in a straight line has no power close to the earth—perhaps because it is broken by hills, stones, and shrubs, and is also hindered by the exhalations of the earth—people throw themselves down when they see the Smum in the distance, in order not to pay with their lives. Often, years are said to pass without the poisonous Smum being felt on the road from Basra to Aleppo <note>original: "Haleb," the historic trade hub in northern Syria.</note>. Nature is also said to have taught the animals to bow their heads to the ground when this wind approaches. When a person is suffocated by this wind, or as the common saying goes, "when his heart has burst," blood is said to sometimes gush from the nose and ears of the deceased two hours later. <meta>This page transitions from climatic observations and sleeping habits to the social and political structure of Arab society, specifically focusing on the concept of nobility and the descendants of Muhammad.</meta>

The Arabs live in cities and villages and in separate families under tents. They have a great number of rulers, most of whom are very proud of their nobility, and they seem to have some reason for this, because their families have ruled independently for several centuries—not, however, because they can prove their nobility through a diploma <note>A formal patent or certificate of rank.</note> received from a powerful Caliph or Sultan; for the Arabs are completely unfamiliar with such a form of granted nobility. Among all Arab families, those descended from **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mohammed"</note> are now the most famous.

The titles of honor bestowed upon these families vary. In Arabia, they are called **Sharif** <note>original: "Scherif"</note> and **Sayyid** <note>original: "Sejid"</note>. In the northern **Muslim** <note>original: "Mohammedan."</note> countries, they are called **Sharif** and **Emir**. In the Arab colonies on the southeastern coast of Africa, in India and Persia, and at **Baghdad** and **Basra**, they are simply called **Sayyid**. At **Hawiza** <note>original: "Hawisa," likely the town of Hoveyzeh in the Khuzestan province of modern Iran.</note>, a small district not far from **Basra**, the ruling lord—who is also a descendant of **Muhammad**—is called **Mawla** <note>original: "Maula," a title signifying a master, protector, or lord.</note>, and if I am not mistaken, this same title is used by the **Sidi** <note>A title of respect, often a dialectal variant of Sayyid.</note> in **Morocco**. In some countries, they have a certain mark of distinction from the

When it is said that the Arabs are very diligent in maintaining their genealogical records <term>original: Geschlechtsregister; family trees or lineages</term>, this is primarily to be understood in relation to the noble Sheikhs, the Sayyids <term>original: Sejids; descendants of the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Husayn</term>, and the Sharifs <term>original: Scherifs; descendants of the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan</term>. Yet even among these, one rarely finds a complete genealogical record spanning many hundreds of years. Similarly (like the Sharifs), the Arab Sheikhs likely also seek to prove their descent only from such persons who have distinguished themselves particularly, and of whom it is generally known that they are already descendants of a famous old family. Various ancient houses, especially among the Bedouin <note>original: Bedouinen</note>, claim—and in some cases there is no doubt at all—that their ancestors were already ruling Sheikhs in the time of Muhammad <note>original: Mohammed</note> and the first Caliphs <note>original: Chalifen; the immediate successors of Muhammad</term>. —

In contrast, the common Arab seldom concerns himself with the name of his grandfather, and likely not even with the name of his father, were it not that the person of the Orient <note>original: Morgenländer; a historical term for people from the Middle East</note> is accustomed to adding the father’s name to his own (for example <note>original Latin abbreviation: e. gr.; exempli gratia</note>, Ali ibn Muhammad, etc.). He also occasionally adopts the name of his city of birth (for example, Ali ibn Muhammad al-Basri <note>original: el Basri; indicating the person is from the city of Basra</note>). Some, especially those [who serve] as slaves among the Muhamm- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "Mohami-", likely "Mohamedanern" or Muslims</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal customs in Yemen regarding homicide and blood revenge. The previous page ended with the family of the victim reserving the right to declare war on the murderer and his relatives.</meta>

relatives, to declare war as it were, and in turn to slay whichever of them they themselves see fit. An honor-loving **Arab** must, however, observe a rough equality of force, and it would be considered shameful for a strong person to attack an elderly or sick person, or for many individuals to set upon a single one. Usually, the most prominent member of the murderer’s family must—if possible—give up his life, as they believe the head of the family is responsible for maintaining order and keeping watch over his kin. 

The murderer himself, meanwhile, is detained and then released by the authorities once he has paid them a certain sum—reportedly 200 <term>Species Thaler</term> <note>A standard silver coinage of the era; the Maria Theresa Thaler was the most common currency used for trade in the Red Sea region and Yemen</note>. This is perhaps the reason why this law has not been abolished. There are said to be examples where such family feuds have lasted for fifty years or more. If, by misfortune, two people from the victim’s side are killed, peace cannot be hoped for until two from the opposing party have shared the same fate—unless an amicable settlement is reached. This highly unjust custom <note>The practice of "blood revenge" (*tha'r*), which often targets a relative of the murderer rather than the murderer himself</note> is forbidden even in the **Quran** <note>The central religious text of Islam, which specifies that only the guilty party should be punished and encourages forgiveness or the acceptance of compensation</note>.

[then], and the oven was covered. Afterwards the bread, which would have seemed barely half-baked to a European, was taken out and eaten while still quite warm. The Arabs in the desert use an iron plate to bake their bread-cakes. Alternatively, they place a round lump of dough into hot coals—made of wood or camel dung—and cover it completely with them until the bread is done in their opinion; then they knock off the ashes and eat it while it is still very warm. The Arabs in the cities have baking ovens roughly similar to our own. These people also do not lack wheat bread. It likewise has the shape and size of our pancakes <note>In this period, "pancakes" often referred to flat, soft rounds of dough rather than the thick, fluffy American style.</note> and is rarely baked long enough. 

The remaining diet of the people of the Orient <note>original: *Morgenländer*; a historical term used to describe people of the East, particularly from the Ottoman Empire and surrounding regions.</note> consists primarily of rice, milk, butter, *kaymak* <note>original: *Cheimak*; a rich, thick clotted cream made from the milk of water buffalo, cows, sheep, or goats.</note> or thick cream, and all sorts of garden fruits. They do not lack meat dishes, but these are consumed only sparingly in hot countries because all meat there is considered unhealthy. They always cook their food under a lid, which makes it very flavorful. It is remarkable that the common man among the Arabs still grinds <note>original: *reibet*; literally "rubs," referring to the process of hand-milling grain between two stones.</note> his bread-grain by hand even today, although the nation [is/has]...

The table of the people of the Orient <note>original: *Morgenländer*; a historical term for people of the East, particularly from the Ottoman Empire and surrounding regions.</note> is arranged according to their manner of living. Since they sit on the ground, they spread a large cloth in the middle of the room on the floor, so that any falling crumbs are not scattered and the carpets <note>original: *Tapeten*; in this historical context, this refers to floor coverings or rugs rather than wallpaper.</note> are not stained. Upon this cloth they place a small stool which supports a large, round copper plate that is heavily tinned; on this plate, the food is served in various small copper bowls, which are always well-tinned both on the inside and the outside.

Among the noble Arabs, instead of napkins, one finds a long cloth which everyone sitting around the table places across their laps. Where this is lacking, each person uses their own small cloth in place of a napkin, which they carry with them to dry themselves after they have washed. They do not use knives and forks—instead, they know how to use their hands so skillfully that they can even do without a spoon when eating milk thickened with bread. I do not remember seeing any other dishes eaten with a spoon <note>original: *Löffelspeisen*; literally "spoon-foods," referring to soups, stews, or thin porridges.</note> among them. (The Turks occasionally have spoons made of wood or horn during their meals.) — — —

He called himself ***Ibrahim Ennasch*** <note>Likely Ibrahim al-Nasikh (Ibrahim the Scribe), a famous 18th-century Coptic calligrapher and icon painter.</note> and was one of the most learned **Copts** in **Cairo** <note>original: *Kahira*</note>, and a very polite man. From him, I learned the following: When the Muslims <note>original: *Mohammedaner*</note> came to **Egypt**, there were 70 bishops of the **Copts**. Now, however, only 13 of them remain. 

1) At **Jerusalem**, 2) at **Bahnesa**, 3) at **Adsjumnein** <note>Ashmunein, the ancient Hermopolis Magna.</note>, 4) at **Menuf**, 5) at **Abutidj** in **Upper Egypt**, 6) at **Girge** in **Upper Egypt**, 7) at **Asiut**, 8) at **Monfalut**, 9) at **Abnubel sammam** <note>Abnub.</note> in **Upper Egypt**, 10) at **Esne** in **Upper Egypt**, 11) at **Armint** in **Upper Egypt**, 12) in ***Habbesch*** <note>Abyssinia (Ethiopia), which historically remained under the jurisdiction of the Coptic Pope of Alexandria until the 20th century.</note>, 13) in **Faiyum**. 

Formerly there was also a bishop in **Cairo**, but since the **Patriarch** himself now resides there, the bishopric has been discontinued. 

7) The aforementioned ***Ibrahim Ennasch*** copied **Coptic** Gospels and other books, together with Arabic...

A Dutchman who had converted to Islam showed me an old inscription in an entirely unknown alphabet, which he had copied in a village—if I am not mistaken—in the district of Belladanes <note>Likely referring to Bilad Anas, a region in Yemen</note>. I have no doubt, therefore, that one may still find Himyaritic <term>Himyaritic: Relating to the ancient Himyarite Kingdom of Yemen, which used a distinct South Arabian script</term> inscriptions in the mountainous regions of Yemen, and particularly between Ta’izz, Sana'a, and Tihamah. However, since I was deathly ill at the time, I forgot to make a copy of the unknown inscription shown to me by the aforementioned Dutchman. 

If I remember correctly, the letters of this script consisted entirely of straight lines; if this is the case, then the Himyarites perhaps received their monumental alphabet from their conquerors, whom they called the <term>Tobba: The "Tubba," a traditional title for the ancient kings of the Himyarites</term> Tobba. These people were from Samarkand and were fire-worshipers <note>A historical term for Zoroastrians</note>—and thus presumably used the very same characters we call "Persepolitan" <note>The author is referring to the cuneiform script found at Persepolis, which at the time was not yet fully deciphered or named as "cuneiform"</note>, because until now they have been found nowhere else but among the ruins of the city of Persepolis. The Himyaritic characters were followed by the Kufic ones <note>An early, angular form of Arabic script</note>, which are still occasionally used today in some regions of the Orient. In Baghdad, a Kufic alphabet is still used for inscriptions at times, in which all the letters are square-shaped.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of writing systems, shifting from the ancient and monumental scripts discussed previously (Himyaritic and Kufic) to the modern calligraphic styles used throughout the Islamic world in the 18th century. The catchword "Die" from the previous page correctly introduces the first sentence here.</meta>

According to the opinion of modern-day Arabs, the newer scripts of the Muslims <note>original: "Mohammedaner"; a historical term for followers of Islam</note> are said to have been invented by a Vizier Ibn Muqla <note>Abu Ali Muhammad ibn Muqla (886–940 AD) was a famous Abbasid official and calligrapher who is credited with refining the geometric proportions of Arabic script</note>, and two of his slaves are said to have popularized them. Yaqut <note>Likely referring to Yaqut al-Musta'simi, a renowned 13th-century calligrapher who refined the six primary scripts</note>, it is said, spread the script known as *Ta'liq* in Persia, and Rihan spread *Naskh* in Arabia. For this reason, even now, the Arabs write all their books in *Naskh* and the Persians commonly in *Ta'liq*. One must admit that the book-copiers of the Orient <note>original: "Morgenländischen"; the author uses this term to refer to the Near East or Islamic world</note> have achieved a very high level of mastery in calligraphy.

The Muslims possess various other styles of book-scripts. The scripts *Thuluth* <note>OCR: "Dtült"</note> or *Rayhani* are a type of ornamental script <note>original: "Fraktur"; the author uses this German term for blackletter as an analogy to describe the bold, formal nature of these scripts</note> used for inscriptions on wood or stone, as well as for the titles of books. In their form, they differ little from *Naskh*. The cursive script of the Turks and Arabs, which those of the middle class <note>original: "Bürgerlichem Stande"</note> use in private letters and accounts, is called *Ruq'ah* <note>OCR: "Rokai"</note>. — *Diwani* is likewise a special style of writing used by the high-ranking Turks or the Ottomans <note>original: "Osmanli"</note>, common primarily in chancelleries and official correspondence. The Imam and the *Qadis* <term>Qadis: Judges who rule in accordance with Islamic religious law</term> like to write their names with interlaced letters so that they cannot be easily forged.

<meta>This page continues the author's observations on the writing and administrative habits of the Islamic world, transitioning from calligraphic styles to the practicalities of correspondence and specialized record-keeping used by the Ottomans and Janissaries.</meta>

The Ottomans <note>original: "Osmanli"</note> sent their letters to other dignitaries in long silk pouches. The Arabs roll them flat to about the width of a thumb and paste the outer end instead of sealing the letter. In the colder regions of Persia, sealing wax is also used, but in the hotter regions, it becomes very warm and soft, so that the signet seal <note>original: "Petschaft"; a hand-held seal used to make an impression in wax</note> becomes unrecognizable.

The Janissaries <note>original: "Janitscharen"; the elite infantry units of the Ottoman Empire</note> use a very special script in their account books, which is called *Siyakat* <note>OCR: "Siaka"; a shorthand script used specifically for financial and land records in the Ottoman administration, known for its complexity and lack of diacritical marks to prevent forgery</note>, and in which the numbers are entirely, but the letters only partially, different from the handwriting of other Muslims <note>original: "Mohammedaner"</note>. —

In certain families in Arabia, one encounters secret scripts and, so to speak, secret languages—with which they can reveal something important to another person without anyone being able to read it except for themselves. Although the Arabian rulers do not spend as much on the sciences as European ones, and for this reason one only rarely finds people in the Orient <note>original: "Morgenländern"; literally the "morning lands"</note> who can rightly be called scholars, the youth among the Muslims are not as neglected as people in Europe perhaps believe. However, one occasionally finds among the **Muslim astrologers** <term>Mohame-danischen Astrologen</term> some who are not entirely unfamiliar with the heavens. The book from which they study is: **The Book of the Fixed Stars** <term>Sur el Kavakeb Labad Abdrach-man es Sofi</term> <note>original: "Suwar al-Kawakib" by Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, a 10th-century Persian astronomer whose work preserved Greek astronomical knowledge and integrated it with traditional Arabic star names.</note>, in which one sees almost all the constellations depicted just as they are in **Bayer’s Uranometria** <term>Bayers Uranometrie</term> <note>A landmark star atlas published in 1603 by Johann Bayer, which introduced the system of naming stars with Greek letters.</note>. They called the **Pole Star** <term>Polarstern</term> **Al-Jady** <term>Dsjudde</term>; **Sirius** was called **Suhail** <term>Suhhel</term>, as well as **Suhail al-Yamani** <term>Suhhel el Jemanie</term>, **Ash-Shi'ra al-Yamani** <term>Esschira el Jema-nie</term> and **Al-Abur** <term>El abur</term>. **Procyon** was **Ash-Shi'ra ash-Shamiyya** <term>Esschira es Sehamie</term>. **Aquila** <note>The Eagle constellation.</note> was **An-Nasr al-Ta’ir** <term>Nisr et Tair</term>. **Lyra** <note>The Lyre constellation.</note> was **An-Nasr al-Waqi** <term>Nisr el Waky</term>, and **Cygnus** <note>The Swan constellation.</note> was **Al-Dajaja** <term>Ded-hadje</term>, that is, the Hen. **Serpentarius** <note>The constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer.</note> was **Al-Hawi** <term>El Gaui</term>. **Cassiopeia** was **Dhat al-Kursi** <term>Saat; el Kursi</term> <note>meaning "The Lady in the Chair."</note>. **Orion** was **Al-Jauza** <term>Ed-sjeuse</term> or **Al-Jabbar** <term>Dsjabar</term> <note>meaning "The Giant."</note>. **Orion's Belt** <term>Baltheus Orionis</term> was **Mintaqat al-Jauza** <term>Mentaket et-sjeusa</term>. **Corona** <note>Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown.</note> was **Alphecca** <term>Elphecca</term>. **Boötes** <term>Booter</term> was **Al-Ramih** <term>Aramächh</term>. **Fomalhaut** <term>Fumhaut</term> was **Fum al-Hut** <term>Fum el haut</term>, that is, the mouth of the fish. **Libra** <note>The Scales.</note> was **Al-Kaffat al-Mizan** <term>Elmaklil Misan</term>. **Berenice’s Hair** <term>Coma Bereaices</term> was **Al-Huzma** <term>El hüsme</term>, that is, the bundle. The **Milky Way** <term>Via lactea</term> was **Nahr al-Majarra** <term>Nahhrel Mudsjerre</term>. The **Pleiades** <term>Pleyades</term> were **Al-Thurayya** <term>Ettorije</term>, and the **Eye of the Bull** <term>Oculus Tauri</term> was **Aldebaran**; but by this they actually mean the stars alpha, gamma, and epsilon <term>Tauri</term> <note>These stars form the "V" shape of the bull's face in the Hyades star cluster.</note>. These were the names of the stars that sound different than they do in **Bayer’s Uranometria**.

In Aleppo <note>original: "Haleb"</note>, comets are called **The Tailed Stars** <note>original: "El Rauakeb el Muſſennabe"</note>, **Lord of the Tails** <note>original: "Sauad el Aſnab"</note>, **Lord of the Beard** <note>original: "Sauad el Lahha"</note>, or **Lord of the Tresses** <note>original: "Sauad eſſauaib"</note>, and so forth. **The Wandering Stars** <note>original: "El Kauakeb el Mutheire"</note> are the planets, and **The Fixed Stars** <note>original: "El Kauakeb et tabita"</note> are the stationary stars. It is not merely the fine opportunity—since the people of the East <note>original: "Morgenländer"</note> often sleep under the open sky—but primarily the lack of clocks that has guided them toward this science... The naming conventions used by the Arabs differ between the scholars and the common folk just as much as they do in Europe....

I have nevertheless encountered some common Arabs who knew various stars; these called the **Great Bear** <note>The constellation Ursa Major.</note> **Ash**, **Nash**, or **The Daughters of Nash** <note>original: "Benat Naſch"; a reference to the Arabic tradition where the three stars of the handle of the Big Dipper are mourners (daughters) following a funeral bier (the four stars of the bowl).</note>. The **Pleiades** they called **Thurayya** <term>Torije</term>; the **Belt of Orion** they called **Mizan** <term>Miſan</term>, which means "the Balance." Another called the stars Delta, Epsilon, and Zeta of Orion <note>These three stars form the famous "Belt" of the hunter Orion.</note> **The True Balance** <term>Miſan elhak</term> and Theta, Delta, and Kappa <note>Stars typically associated with the "Sword" or lower portion of the constellation.</note> **The False Balance** <term>Miſan el Batel</term>. Some called the **Pole Star** **Al-Qutb** <note>original: "Kattab," meaning the Axis or Pole.</note>, while others called it **Al-Jady** <note>original: "Dsjüddi," meaning the Young Goat or Kid.</note>.

The two large stars in the **Little Bear** <note>Ursa Minor; these stars are Beta and Gamma Ursae Minoris, often called the "Guardians of the Pole."</note> are called **Heissen** <term>Heiſſen</term> by the sailors on the **Persian Gulf**. In that same region, **Cassiopeia** was called **Jahhi**. **Venus**, which we see in the evening after sunset, these Arabs called **Maghribi** <term>Marebi</term>, that is, the evening star. **Aldebaran** <note>The brightest star in the constellation Taurus.</note> was called in this region **Suwayq al-Thurayya** <note>original: "Soik et torije"; meaning "The Follower of the Pleiades," as it appears to follow that star cluster across the sky.</note>. Among the common folk, however, one still hears the fable that the celestial bodies, during their darkening, are eclipsed by a great fish. Women and children then make a great noise on their rooftops with their copper and brass vessels in order to chase the fish away. They also tell where this fable comes from. Only very few astronomers are able to calculate anything according to the tables of Ulugh Beg <note>Ulugh Beg (1394–1449) was a Timurid ruler and astronomer who produced one of the most accurate star catalogs of the Middle Ages.</note>—the Parsi <note>original: "Parsi"; referring to Zoroastrians or "fire-worshippers."</note> also use these tables, however. Because Muhammad <note>original: "Mohamed"</note> forbade seeking counsel through lots and divining by arrows, this ancient custom is no longer found among the Arabs. Bloodletting is also known in Arabia—but cupping <term>Schröpfen: a treatment where glass cups are heated and applied to the skin to create suction</term> is more common among the Arabs. — The southern Arabs maintain that anointing strengthens the body—and also helps in cases of illness. — Extreme Unction <term>Oehlung: the anointing of the sick with oil, often called "Last Rites"</term> among Eastern Christians is not performed until there is no longer any hope of recovery. — The people of the Orient <note>original: "Morgenländer"</note> do not know much of toothaches, presumably because they diligently clean their mouths whenever they have eaten fruit or other foods. <meta>This page transitions from health observations (the absence of plague and the practice of smallpox inoculation) to the mineral resources of Arabia, discussing the scarcity of gold, alchemical interests, and the presence of iron and lead mines.</meta>

In Yemen the plague is not found . . . The women of the Bedouins inoculate their children against smallpox <note>original: "Blattern"; this refers to variolation, an early method of immunization where material from a smallpox sore was scratched into the skin of a healthy person</note> themselves, and for lack of a better instrument, they use a thorn bush to scratch the poor little arms . . . In Arabia there is little gold, hence the Arabs sometimes develop a desire for alchemy <term>Goldmacherkunst: literally "the art of gold-making," the historical practice of attempting to transform base metals into gold</term>. . . . The aforementioned Maronite <note>A member of an Eastern Catholic Christian community primarily from Lebanon</note> related: that in the region of and on Mount Lebanon (and in Yemen) a herb is found that the goats like to eat, and that stains their teeth golden-yellow. The juice of this herb had once made his handkerchief so brittle that one could rub it to pieces with one's fingers. He rubbed the silver on his saber with this herb, and it became golden-yellow, but after a few days it became white again.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on agricultural productivity, specifically concluding the thought from the previous page regarding high-yield wheat harvests before shifting to discuss the cultivation of Durra and general agricultural conditions in the Near East and Yemen.</meta>

as was assured, wheat yields a hundredfold. — This may well have also applied here and there to the Jewish land <note>referring to Judea or Palestine</note>. However, Herodotus in Book 1, 182 <note>original: "Herod. lib. I. 182."</note> and the Holy Scripture in the passages where they speak of hundredfold increase, perhaps speak only of the increase of Durra <term>Durra: a species of sorghum or millet common in arid climates, known for its resilience and high yield</term>. The common Arabs taste almost no other bread than that made from Durra. — Because the soil in the various regions of the Orient <note>German: "Morgenland," a historical term for the East</note> is not uniform, and the weather is often very diverse, the land is also cultivated in various ways. — In Egypt, Palestine, Syria, and Mesopotamia, many fields lie uncultivated due to a lack of inhabitants; and it seems that little diligence is applied to agricultural work. The tools of the farmers in the aforementioned lands, as well as in Arabia and India, are very poor.

It seems that the fields in Yemen are cultivated quite well, and in some regions even as meticulously as a garden. ### I. The Land of Yemen. <note>original: "Ard el Jemen"</note>

Nature has divided the landscape into two parts: a) the low-lying <term>Tehama</term> <note>The Tihama is the hot, arid coastal plain bordering the Red Sea</note>, and b) the higher or mountainous region—<term>Dsgåbbal</term> <note>A phonetic rendering of the Arabic *jabal*, meaning mountain; here referring to the fertile Yemeni highlands</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Yemen’s history and terminology, following the author’s inquiry into the country's ancient inhabitants and religious changes.</meta>

The word *Tobba* <note>Tubba; an ancient title for the kings of the Himyarite Kingdom</note>, however, was thought by some to have been a title of honor for the ancient Arabian rulers, just as *Pharaoh* was among the *Egyptians*. In *Muscat*, *Tobba* and *Hamjar* <note>Himyar</note> are still common names for individual *Arabs* today. In the region of *Cheivan* <note>Khaywan</note>, one also occasionally finds an ancient family that bears the name *Tobba* and perhaps descends from the old *Yemeni* kings. An Arabian scholar in *Mocha* <note>Al Mukha</note> was of the opinion that in ancient times, only the *Yemeni* kings who were originally from *Samarkand* and had been fire-worshipers <note>A historical term often used to describe Zoroastrians</note> held the title *Tobba*.

I diligently inquired after books in *Yemen*, and the most distinguished historical works were indeed shown to me, but people did not wish to sell them, and there was no time for transcribing them. The books mentioned are: *Bork el Jemen* <note>original: "al-Barq al-Yamani" (The Yemeni Lightning), a history of the Ottoman conquest</note>; *Karat elajun* <note>original: "Qurrat al-Uyun" (Delight of the Eyes)</note>, *Nefais el arais* <note>original: "Nafa'is al-ara'is" (The Jewels of the Brides)</note> etc. The first two are said to be the primary books on the history of *Yemen*. The throne of **Yemen** is hereditary—however, the eldest prince does not always necessarily succeed to the government. Furthermore, the **Imam** <note>The title of the ruler of Yemen</note> of **Yemen** is a free ruler, independent in both spiritual and worldly matters—He adheres to the **Zaydi** sect <note>A branch of Shia Islam</note> and is to be regarded as the spiritual head in his country.

The subjects of the **Imam** belonging to the **Sunni** sect are under a **Mufti** <note>A Muslim legal expert empowered to give rulings on religious law</note> at **Zabid**; the latter is presumably under the **Sunni** **Kadi** <note>A judge who presides over matters of Islamic law</note> at **Sana'a**.

The inhabitants, especially those who live on high mountains, are said to speak excellent Arabic because they have almost no contact with foreigners; their dialect is said to most closely resemble the language used in the Koran. However, they know almost nothing of the Koran itself beyond its name. On these mountains, Arab women do not marry before the age of 15, and a man rarely has more than one wife. Their diet consists of meat, honey, milk, and herbs. — They live to a great age and maintain sharp eyesight.

## II. The Land of Hadhramaut.

It is very large. In ancient times, the two regions of Hadhramaut and Yemen were known as **Fortunate Arabia** <note>original: "das glückliche Arabien," translating the Latin *Arabia Felix*. This name was given by Greeks and Romans because the region was much more fertile and wealthy—due to the frankincense trade—than the rest of the peninsula</note>. ——— The **Sunni** <note>One of the two main branches of Islam</note> sect is the dominant one. The dialect is so very different from that of Yemen that I once had to speak with these Arabs through an interpreter. They pride themselves somewhat on their scholarship and religion; however, the Yemenis do not judge them so favorably. **Giggeius** <note>Likely Antonius Giggeius, a 17th-century scholar known for his monumental Arabic-Latin dictionary</note> holds the dialect in great contempt. — One finds many independent lordships in this region. The **Bedouin** <note>Nomadic desert dwellers</note> are under the rule of a multitude of free **Sheikhs**; as are the **Qaba'il** <note>original: "Kobail" — referring to the tribal peoples, specifically those who inhabit mountainous areas</note>.

## III. The Land of Oman.

It is mountainous and divided into various small, independent lordships. The **Imam** of Oman is the most powerful. The land is fertile in wheat, barley, maize, lentils, and three varieties of grapes (which are called **Raske Helali** and **Bagal Helali**); dates, etc. It is also productive in livestock.

## IV. Independent Lordships on the Persian Gulf.

The Arabs on the Persian coast lead almost entirely the same way of life. They sustain themselves through seafaring, pearl diving, and fishing. Their food consists of dates, durra bread <note>A bread made from sorghum, a grain common in arid regions</note>, and fish; indeed, even their few livestock live primarily on fish. They are as zealous defenders of their freedom as their brothers in the desert. Almost every city has its independent Sheikh <note>original: "Scheck"</note>, to whom they pay almost no taxes at all.

Their weapons consist of a musket with a matchlock, a saber, and a shield. All still speak the Arabic language today. Most are Sunnis <note>Followers of the Sunni branch of Islam</note> and, for that reason alone, are born enemies of the Persians <note>Who followed the Shia branch, creating a long-standing religious and political tension in the region</note>. Their houses are so poor that an enemy would not even take the trouble to tear them down. In general, they do not have much to lose on the land. Therefore, when a Persian army advances against them, they abandon their land and retreat to an island for as long as it takes for the Persians to withdraw. In doing so, they are certain that their enemies cannot cultivate their land because of the neighboring Arabs. In short, the form of government and the way of life of these Arabs have much in common with those of the ancient Greeks <note>The author likely refers to the decentralized, independent city-states of ancient Greece, which were also seafaring and fiercely protective of their autonomy</note>.

## VIII. Various Tribes of Bedouins or Wandering Arabs.

The city dwellers <note>original: "Städer"; referring to the settled populations in urban centers</note> have, through mixing with foreigners, lost a great deal of their ancient customs and manners. The true Arabs, who have at all times valued their freedom higher than wealth and comfort, live in separate tribes in tents, and still constantly observe the ancient form of government, manners, and habits of their ancestors. Their nobles they call <term>Sheikh</term> <note>original: "Schech" or "Schächh"; an Arabic title signifying an elder or leader of a tribe</note>. A Sheikh rules over his family and all their servants. If these cannot defend their property against their neighbors, then several smaller Sheikhs unite and choose a greater one from among themselves. Several greater Sheikhs may, with the approval of the smaller ones, subject themselves to one even greater and more powerful than they; namely a <term>Sheikh el-kebir</term> <note>original: "Schächh el kbir"; meaning the Great Sheikh</note> or <term>Sheikh el-Shuyukh</term> <note>original: "Schächh es Schiech"; meaning the Sheikh of Sheikhs</note>, and the entire tribe is then named after the family of this great Sheikh. They are all, as it were, born soldiers and at the same time engage in animal husbandry. The Sheikhs of the large tribes have a multitude of camels, partly to use them in their wars, partly to carry the merchants' goods from one city to another, and partly to sell them. The smaller and, so to speak, subordinate tribes raise more sheep. Agriculture and other heavy labor they leave to

<note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "lassen" indicates the sentence continues on the next page, likely explaining that they leave labor to slaves or peasants.</note>

<meta>This page continues the description of Bedouin social structures and their nomadic lifestyle, picking up from the previous page's discussion of how labor is divided within the tribes.</meta>

<page-num>506</page-num>

they leave to their subjects, the common Arabs. These live in poor huts, while the Sheikhs live in tents. Since these Arabs are always in the open air, they have an exceedingly keen sense of smell. Cities do not please them at all, and they cannot comprehend how people can live in them, amidst such impurity of the air. They are said to live for five days without water, and can immediately determine how deep they must dig in a spot to find water, simply by looking at the soil and the herbs growing therein. In short, they are very skilled at raids <note>original: "Streifereyen"; referring to nomadic excursions or skirmishes</note> in the desert. The government remains within the family of every great and small <term>Sheikh</term>, and it is not always the eldest son who receives leadership, but rather the one who is most capable—even if it were another close relative. They pay little or nothing to their superiors. These Bedouins have never been conquered by foreigners and will never be conquered.

The various tribes wage many wars among themselves, but these are neither bloody nor long-lasting. But as soon as one among them is attacked by a foreign enemy—namely the Turk <note>referring to the Ottoman Empire, which sought to exert control over the peninsula</note>—they quickly unite to defend the common good first. Each of them believes himself to be completely sovereign in his territory, because his ancestors in the region where he lives,

The various tribes of the Arabs, of which I have received reports, are the following:

## Haoma Yasht <note>original: "Heomo Verekehe"; this refers to a specific hymn or liturgical section of the Avesta dedicated to the sacred plant-deity Haoma.</note>

---

Around the *Havani Gah* <note>original: "Gah-Havan"; the first of the five periods of the Zoroastrian day, occurring between sunrise and noon</note>, *Haoma* <note>original: "Hom"; the personification of the sacred ritual plant</note> descended from the heights to *Zoroaster* <note>The prophet Zarathustra</note> and found him cleaning the fire temple and reading the word of *Ahura Mazda* <note>original: "Ormusd"; the supreme creator deity in Zoroastrianism</note>. I, Zoroaster, asked him: to which man who lives in righteousness as Zoroaster does, has it been granted by you to keep his soul pure and immortal?

The pure, death-destroying Haoma answered me: I, O Zoroaster, am the pure Haoma, the death-destroyer; whoever speaks to me, O *Spitaman* <note>original: "Sapatman"; the clan name or patronymic of Zoroaster</note>, whoever consumes me, calls to me with the ardor of fire, and offers me humble prayer—he receives from me the goods of the world.

Then Zoroaster spoke: I pray to Haoma. Who, O Haoma, is the first mortal in the created world who, through invocation and humility, has received from you that which he yearns for?

The pure, death-destroying Haoma answered: *Vivanghat* <note>original: "Vivengham"; a mythological figure in the Avesta, father of Yima (Jamshid), and the first mortal to prepare the Haoma juice</note> is the first mortal in the created world who called upon me in humility, and
